WELCOME TO MEMBER FOR WATERLOO SOUTH ON HIS RETURN AFTER SERIOUS ILLNESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house frequently takes time to pay tribute to one of its members who has died. This day I should like to pay tribute to one of its members who has refused to die.
The presence here today of my deskmate, the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth), is a tribute not only to Canadian surgery, but also to a great and fighting heart.

subtopic: INTEGRATED PLAN

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert H. Winters (Minister of Reconstruction and Supply):
subtopic: INTEGRATED PLAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Thursday, February 24, 1 advised the house that the integrated housing plan was under review in the hope that some modified form could be arrived at to overcome certain difficulties which had occurred in isolated cases during 1948. For reasons which I will mention, no applications for integrated housing contracts have been accepted since December 31, 1948. It has now been decided, however, to proceed with the plan, with certain changes.
The integrated housing plan was developed in 1945 to encourage builders to construct moderate-priced houses for sale to veterans. Under the plan the builder entered into an agreement with the corporation by which he agreed to build a specified number of houses of a certain type or types, and to offer them for sale to veterans at or under the maximum selling price set out in the agreement.
Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for its part agreed to arrange priority assistance for the builder, and to purchase any house that he was unable to sell to a prospective house owner, at a price which would cover the estimated costs of construction and the cost of the land upon which it was built.
The agreement required that the builder should finance the construction of his houses by loans under the National Housing Act. Thus the plan consisted of an agreement
between the contractor and the corporation, which refers only to the sale price to the purchasers and the corporation's commitment to repurchase. On the strength of the agreement, the builder obtained the financing from lending institutions who were doing business under the National Housing Act.
More than 13,000 units have been undertaken under the plan, and almost all of those completed have been sold. We have acquired under our repurchase commitment forty-three housing units, as of the end of the year. Despite the fact that the plan has for the most part gone well, there has been adverse criticism because of the fact that some veterans -about one hundred in all-have been in danger of losing down payments made to the builder, or have had to pay higher prices than contemplated by reason of the contractor being unable to complete the house because he experienced financial difficulties. The plan is in essence a price-fixing arrangement, and there is no direct contact between the purchaser and the corporation. Nevertheless some purchasers have relied on an assumption that the agreement between the builder and the corporation would give them protection, and have not taken normal precautions in their dealings with the builders. While there is nothing in the arrangement that justifies this assumption, the government feels that it would not be prudent to proceed with the plan without taking steps to correct this situation by reducing the possibility of its recurrence and making provision for remedial action where failure does occur in the future. To accomplish this purpose I believe that contractors should not accept down payments before completion of the house, or alternatively, that down payments accepted before completion of the house and its delivery to the prospective purchaser should be trusteed. In addition a provision must be included which will permit the corporation to obtain control of the property as soon as difficulties of the kind mentioned occur, so that remedial action may be taken.
Because of the foregoing, and because it is desired to have the integrated plan proceed, the following modifications will be made:
(a)	Provision will be made in the integrated agreement that sales shall not be finalized until the house is at least ninety per cent completed.
1140	HOUSE OF
Inquiries of the Ministry
(b)	That down payments by the purchaser shall be placed in trust immediately by the contractor until the completion of the sales transaction and the delivery of possession to the purchaser.
(c)	That in support of his application for mortgage advances the builder shall produce paid bills for construction materials that have gone into the house, or lien waivers from the suppliers of such materials.
(d)	That the builder shall deliver to the corporation, when the house has reached the first-floor joist stage of construction, a conveyance of the property, to be held by the corporation until a sale has been arranged to a prospective house owner, or until the property is taken over by the corporation under its commitment to purchase it from the builder. This will give the corporation effective control of the property during the period of construction.
(e)	Because most builders rely upon down payments, now to be trusteed, for working capital, the corporation shall advance to the builder at the time it gets the conveyance- that is, at the first-floor joist stage of construction-the difference between the loan under the National Housing Act and the sale price to the corporation. This amounts to approximately half the down payment that will be made by the purchasers. This sum will be recovered by the corporation from the builder on sale of the property to the prospective house owner.
The arrangement which I have outlined introduces a number of new features which are restrictive to builders, and we have not yet received the reaction of the trade. Accordingly we will again review the plan as to its manner of working and in the light of the veteran demand for houses under it.

should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister. To those of us who come from the farthest parts of the country the date and length of the Easter recess may be of greater interest than they are to those who are privileged to go home over the week ends. In view of the variety of opinion expressed in

the press as to the possible length of the recess, is the Prime Minister in position to let us in on the secret?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There is no secret about it. I have been talking to the whip on our side, and he tells me that he has been discussing the matter with various members but finds that there is perhaps as great a divergence of opinion as there is in the newspaper stories. No decision has been arrived at, but it does seem to me that we have to choose between a short recess at Easter, perhaps from Good Friday to Easter Monday, and one that would give hon. members from all parts of the country an opportunity to go home if they saw fit to do so, thus necessitating a recess of a couple of weeks.
I think if we are to have the longer recess it might be just as well to take both the week before Easter and Easter week. In any event they are both only partial weeks. Such a recess would give hon. members from all parts of the country time to get to their respective homes and have a few days there before being required to come back. The choice between the alternatives will probably have to depend upon what progress we can make in the meantime, because the business of parliament will have to be discharged. I hope we shall have made such progress that the longer recess will appear to be justified, not only to ourselves but to the public.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REPORTED DECLARATION OF WHEAT AS SURPLUS IN UNITED STATES
speechtext: I should like to ask the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) a question. Has the government any statement to make on the recent report by Charles F. Brennan, secretary of agriculture in President Truman's cabinet, that he was declaring wheat a surplus commodity in the United States under the European recovery program? What reduction will it make in-or will it eliminate entirely-Marshall plan dollars for the purchase in Canada of non-American wheat? How will it affect Canada?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: REPORTED DECLARATION OF WHEAT AS SURPLUS IN UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Information did come to us this morning, although not officially, about this statement by the secretary of agriculture in the United States that wheat was surplus. We were somewhat disturbed about it, although it would appear that the appropriations being urged upon congress at the present time for United States dollars in aid of the recovery of the United Kingdom are not being reduced.
Inquiries of the Ministry
Of course those United States dollars are important, perhaps essential, to the recovery of the United Kingdom; but they are only a portion of the dollars the United Kingdom government has for its requirements abroad It may be that it is more important to the United Kingdom that the number of United States dollars under ERP remain the same than it is to have them attributed to any special commodity.
I hope that whatever is done will not affect the capacity of the United Kingdom to carry out those contracts it has made with us, both for 1948-49 and for 1949-50. It should not affect the capacity of the United Kingdom to carry out those contracts if the same number of ERP dollars is available to pay for part of the requirements of commodities the United Kingdom must import.

subtopic: REPORTED DECLARATION OF WHEAT AS SURPLUS IN UNITED STATES

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when the house rose last night I had been dealing with a number of subjects, one of which was the policy of the government in respect to improving health facilities throughout Canada. I had referred to a number of orders in council that had been passed by the government. One particular order in council provided for an increase-

speechtext: Order. I must say to hon. members that there is so much noise in the house that the hon. member who has the floor cannot be heard.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

One of those orders in council authorizes an expenditure of money in excess of the amount appropriated by parliament. Such a practice cannot be too strongly condemned. Another order in council divided the appropriation for hospital construction grants among the provinces according to the population of the province based on the 1947 intercensal estimates. Of the total of $'13 million available, that basis of division gave $3,842,650 to the province of Quebec; but, according to answers tabled yesterday by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), the province of Quebec has had approved not $3,842,650 but $5,427,552. I do not object to the province of Quebec getting that sum of money if it is voted by parliament. I would support such a move, but I do object to the government's approving for hospital construction in any province an amount of money larger than the amount approved by parliament and allocated by order in council.
I should like to refer to another part of the speech of the Minister of National Health and Welfare in which I think he was attempting to take unto himself and the government a great deal more credit than they deserve. On page 839 of Hansard he said:
I feel I may say that the new energy put into research by the national cancer institute and the national health program brings the money available for health research this year to an all-time record of more than $1,250,000.
Last session the government asked parliament to approve for health research an amount of only $100,000. Of the $100,000, up until the end of the first eleven months of the present fiscal year only $5,850 had been spent. The minister is shaking his head, but if he will look at the return that was tabled yesterday he will see that is correct.
I have it in my hand, and it shows that the total spent for public health research is something less than $6,000. With an expenditure of less than $6,000, the Minister of National Health and Welfare is attempting to take credit for an expenditure of more than one and a quarter million dollars for health


research. I submit that the whole speech of the minister was a gross exaggeration when dealing with the government's supposed accomplishments.
I also discussed to some extent last night the wheat policy of the government, and I was about to refer to the stand taken by the leader of the C.C.F. group, the member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), when the Canada-United Kingdom wheat agreement was being debated in the house. I quote from page 4825 of Hansard of August 15, 1946:
I believe the government would be well advised to consider this suggestion: that, in the event of the costs of production rising for the next few years, as they will do largely because of the government's failure to maintain the ceilings, any difference there may be between what the farmer receives for his wheat and the increased cost of production should be made up out of the consolidated revenue fund of Canada.
Costs of production were much lower in August 1946 than they are today. The general wholesale price index, which is the index of the prices of all commodities, was 109-3 at that time. The index for January 1949 is up to 159-3, an increase of 50 points. The C.C.F. group believes that a compensatory payment should be made to farmers, and if it is made on the basis of the increase of 50 points in the wholesale index, then farmers should be given at least an additional payment of 71 cents a bushel.
Our farmers believed that when the price for the last year of the wheat agreement was being discussed a figure would be decided upon taking into consideration the "have regard" clause, the clause which says that towards the end of the contract a figure for the last year will be arrived at which will take into consideration whether or not the prices in the first years of the contract were below world prices. We shall soon be facing a general election. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) knows very well that the most important issue in the prairie provinces in any election is the question of wheat prices. If he expected to obtain a substantial payment on account of the "have regard" clause, I think an announcement would already have been made. I submit that the "have regard" clause amounts to very little, and possibly will amount to nothing-not through any fault of the British, because Britain cannot pay dollars she does not possess. I say, however, that the government should have regard to the farmers of Canada, and because of the "have regard" clause in the contract the government should see to it that the farmers receive a fair price for their wheat, a price in accordance with world prices that have prevailed for the duration of the contract.

I was sorry to hear the announcement by the Prune Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) in which I understood him to state that wheat was being declared a surplus commodity in the United States. I am afraid this action may place our whole British market in jeopardy. As I have understood it from press reports in the past, as soon as any agricultural product is declared surplus in the United States, ERP dollars cease to be available for the purchase of that commodity in any country other than the United States. If that policy is followed I am afraid our whole wheat market is in serious danger.
Another question of deep concern to the people of the prairies is the adoption of a scheme which will adequately protect them in time of crop failure. At every session since I became a member of parliament I have asked for changes in the Prairie Farm Assistance Act which would make payments available on an individual basis. The government surely know that under the present act many farmers are discriminated against, though in fact they have crop failures, because they cannot come within the provisions of the act. One farmer may have a complete crop failure, but because the farmers around him had good crops he cannot qualify for the prairie farm assistance payments. I have received a number of complaints about this legislation in the past, but this session I had a new one. Farmers in a particular township where the yield was just over eight bushels per acre complained that other surrounding townships received prairie farm assistance payments, but that since none of the townships directly alongside them qualified, they were unable to qualify under the act. These farmers pointed out that townships diagonally across from them received the payments, and that portions of townships alongside them were declared within the bonus area, but they were excluded. Therefore while blocks of other townships in the immediate vicinity were brought under the provisions of the act, the farmers in the particular township of which I speak could not qualify for these crop failure payments.
The whole act needs to be completely revised. There have been many inequalities in the past, and there will be many more in the future if the act is not completely overhauled so that payments may be made on an individual basis. Only in this way can fairness and equity be brought about. On the basis of present prices and costs of production the maximum payment of $2.50, even if it is obtained, is far short of being sufficient to provide the farmer with enough money to carry on his operations. Again this session, as I have done at every previous session since
The Address-Mr. Reid I first came here, I urge that the payment should be increased from a maximum of $2.50 an acre to at least $6, and that payments should be on an individual basis.
I see, Mr. Speaker, that my time has expired. There are many other problems I should have liked to discuss, but I shall deal with them at another time.

The Address-Mr. Reid ter would agree that he was careful to give every bit of credit possible to the various provincial governments for what they have done in the matter of health. I do not think it is fair to say the minister was taking glory to himself.
The hon. member said that the $30 million health program had been in effect for eleven months. That is the first error in mathematics I am going to correct. That was the first misstatement. Then the hon. member went a little further and tried the old trick we have seen before of setting *one province against another. He mentioned the province of Quebec and what it is getting, but there again he was all wrong. If he had been more careful and not so biased, with his mind made up to simply damage and criticize the government, he might have noticed the difference between allotment and expenditure. Under the new national health program introduced and being carried out under the able administration of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, the allotment for hospitals is on a cumulative basis. This enables any provincial government to come forward with a one or even five year hospital scheme if that is their desire; but no provincial government will receive more at the end of five years than it is entitled to under the national health program.
To make the statement that the province of Quebec has got away with more money than the province of Saskatchewan is untrue, Mr. Speaker, in the light of the actual facts. If the hon. member was not aware of it, he should have been.

I maintain there are some members of parliament who are leading the people up false channels. We have heard a lot about bribery to win elections. When I came to this land away back in 1909, a land which by the way has been very good to me, I was told that I was going to the land of promise. It seems to me however that it is becoming of late a land of promises. I can speak freely of it because, since I entered public life since 1922, I have made only one promise in my life, and that one has been faithfully kept. That was a promise to give the utmost of my services to all the citizens. There again I think of the old Presbyterian doctrine, that it is better not to promise, and do, than it is to promise and not fulfil.
We hear hon. members rise in their places and dangle promises before the people, and yet they talk about bribery. Is there any name for these false promises except bribery? No; it is worse than bribery. Because, if a government has spent money here or there, the people have got it; but many of these things which are being promised, the people may never get. Shortly I shall challenge any member to get up and tell me which expenditures of government he would reduce. However, before asking him to do so, may I say there is one other procedure I cannot understand, when people say, "Do not pay your debts. Just leave the national debt, and pay no attention to it at all." Well, I am one who has endeavoured during a lifetime to pay his debts, and this suggestion does not appeal to me greatly. At the present time the interest on our public debt is $445 million; then we have subsidies to the provinces of $100 million; family allowances, $270 million; veterans payments, $300 million; old age pensions, $65 million; post office, $75 million; public works, $70 million; national health program, $30 million; defence of Canada, $250 million. All these total $1,605 million. Then, the total taxes in 1948, taken in excess profits and income tax amounted to $1,286,878,849. That is away below even the ordinary commitments at the present time.
I challenge any member to rise in his place and tell me which of the items I have enumerated he would be in favour of reducing. When he gets up to speak he can tell us how you can reduce taxes and increase expenditures.

I have never changed my position on old age pensions. I am glad the hon. member mentioned this matter, for I want a better deal for these pensioners. Some interesting speeches have been delivered this session against communism. I am one of those who believe that we can never stop the growth of communism in this country by merely crying "bad wolf". Let me give another illustration. During the Yale by-election both the Liberals and the Conservatives devoted a lot of time, both on the platform and over the radio, to an attempt to warn the people against communism. One has only to look at the results of the vote to see how much attention was paid to that cry.
I do not generally refer to it as communism. I have asked some of those who belong to the L.P.P. in what countries communism is being practised today. I know of no country where it is being practised. It is true that some countries started out under Karl Marx doctrines, but no country has so far operated that way. What they have in Russia today is Stalinism, not Karl Marxism. I would say that the great menace facing the world today is soviet imperialism.
I was astounded at the attitude of certain men in the greater Vancouver area over a statement which I had made with regard to a proposed visit of two Russian scientists to investigate what the international Pacific salmon fisheries commission had done at Hell's Gate and throughout the province. Word to that effect came from the United States embassy to the embassy here and each member of the commission was asked if he was agreeable to this visit being made. As one of the three Canadian members I was asked and I said, "No, I have no objection to anyone coming, but if they come I think it would be only fair to ask the soviet to allow two of our scientists to go there to see what they are doing in connection with fisheries". As I say, I was astounded at the reaction of that statement. I received terrible letters of abuse from certain people in and around the greater Vancouver area. I was called all kinds of names. I did not think there was anything unfair in saying to a country, "We will show you what we have if you in turn will show us what you have". I was abused for taking that attitude.
I have linked up these two questions for the moment. There have been many faults in capitalism or free enterprise. Looking back over history we find that there are some pages that are not so bright. However, up to the present time that system has given man more of this world's goods and more freedom than any other system. But we will have to adopt some new rules in the game.

m order to control the greed of some men more than we have in the past. Coming now to old age pensions, I believe that the people of this country are demanding more along the lines of social security. I should like to see far more of it in this country. I am of the firm belief that if that were done we would stop the spread of this thing that is termed communism.
Before I close I should like to say just one word with regard to trade. I am sorry I have not the time to go into this more fully because I feel it might be a contribution. Great Britain has been our best customer. What I say now is in no carping sense to the members of the C.C.F. I am delighted to see that they are now great supporters of the British, but there were times when that was not quite so evident. I want to remind them that we on this side of the house have just as much good feeling for the people of the British Isles, even though they are now under a Labour government, as any other group in the house. It is to our benefit and interest that we do everything we can to see that that great market for our wheat and other products is not lost.
I am not a financier, but there have been times when I have spoken in this house about silver bimetalism. There were days when we were pinning our faith on metals, but I have learned since that the faith of man can be used to successfully carry out the exchange of goods between nations without the use of precious metals. But we are now faced with an impasse. Contrary to general opinion, I am one of those who believe that our Canadian dollar is not tied to anything. Many believe that the Canadian dollar is tied to the United States dollar, but I contend that we have a dollar of our own. However, all you have to do is to try to exchange it across the line and you will find that they are not ready to take it. With our adverse balance of trade we have to pay the United States the coin they want.
Many countries including the soviet union still put their faith in gold. No one knows the gold holdings of the soviet empire, but accounts come out of that country that they are searching feverishly for gold. It may well be that they are able to do a lot of trading with gold. I wonder what the United States is going to do with the 25,000 tons of gold it has buried in vaults? That is what it works out to. The United States has eighty per cent of the world's gold and with gold valued at $35 per ounce they have a total value of $25,000 million. Without knowing what the Russian holdings are, the world's gold supply is said to be around $28,000 million.
The Address-Mr. Blair
I am just wondering if we are going to continue forever to pay men to dig into the earth to find gold and then transport it across the line to bury it again in the earth? That seems to be all that can be done with it. In the case of most countries-Switzerland is one exception-and this applies to Great Britain particularly, the supply of gold for exchange is gradually dwindling. I am wondering if the United States should not break the impasse by again redistributing the gold chips, shall I say, to the various nations? So long as we continue to talk about sterling and United States dollars, so long as we do not get any closer than that, there is little hope for an improvement in our trading position.
Let me remind my friends in the C.C.F. that the Labour government has departed from the old traditions. Great Britain was built up with free trade, but now the Labour government is carrying on by means of quotas. That is not generally recognized. Trading by quotas means that they pick out from that country or this country certain quantities of goods. Therein lies some of the difficulty in connection with our trading relations with Great Britain.
I am sorry my time is exhausted as I would like to have dealt with this matter in detail. I rose principally to correct the record and to put it straight as to the government's national health program.

Mr. Speaker, it is quite apparent that this Friday afternoon is health day in the House of Commons. I am delighted that the debate has taken this form. For years I have tried to use the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne as a vehicle to talk to the members, and to try to bring before them the necessity for some action to bring about betterment of health conditions in Canada, and a definite health plan for Canada. For this I offer no apology. It is not so much because of my own interest in these matters as it is that I realize there are conditions in Canada, the high cost of hospitalization and the lack of opportunity for treatment, that make it a matter which should receive the attention of all members.
We must recognize today that, with nations as with individuals, we are faced with the fact of the survival of the fittest, and if Canada does not raise the standard of health of her citizens to a maximum equal to that of any other nation she will fall by the wayside in international affairs. We must recognize a nation's health at its full value, not only from the human point of view, but from the economic side as well. We must realize that money spent on health is money saved.

The Address-Mr. Blair Sickness and disease do not stop at provincial boundaries. A disease of epidemic proportions in one district may readily spread to another province. Only those who are not conversant with the facts will quarrel with the spending of public money to care for the health of the people. Surely no one thinks that we can afford to go on losing money as we are today on account of sickness, simply because we are spending such a small amount publicly on prevention.
Death, disease and sickness are proportionate to the amount of money spent on health services. Society has two responsibilities with regard to sickness. One is the adoption of curative measures, and the other is the adoption of preventive measures. The history of our health services in Canada shows that up to the present time we have been paying more attention to curative measures than we have to preventive measures. We have not achieved the results that will follow if we pay more attention to preventive measures.
It is almost 200 years since Jenner discovered vaccination and made the conquest of smallpox possible. At that time the average duration of life was thirty years; now it is close to seventy. But still there are thousands of people who are dying unnecessarily each year, largely because they lack the opportunity for treatment. I emphasize that phrase, "the opportunity for treatment." There is a growing demand from the public for release from the ever-present possibility of the high cost of hospitalization or sickness.
The doctor in general practice today is very often faced with the problem of giving adequate treatment or adequate diagnosis. The facilities are not there for him. The duty of the state is to care for those who by reason of infirmity are incapacitated as far as gainful employment is concerned, and those who unfortunately cannot afford to pay for treatment.
We recognize today the importance of education and health. These two subjects are very close together, and the standard of living is also an adjunct. It may be said that people are becoming too prone to take advantage of free clinics, and that they try to get as much as possible for nothing. This is not a reasonable attitude. Most of us wish to give them the best in legislation for the benefit of all people without breeding a class of people who lose their self-reliance. We are aware of the deficiencies in our present health set-up, but we must be careful to take the proper steps towards the right kind of program. We should be aware of the financial plight of our hospitals, and the necessity both for new buildings and for extensions. We should be aware of the prohibitively high 
cost, to patients, of hospital care. We should be aware of the difficulty of a large part of our population in obtaining treatment services, both curative and preventive.
Hospitals should be houses of healing with a sound financial atmosphere. Unfortunately that does not exist in Canada. Hospital boards are left in anxiety and despair to maintain their institutions. We have been too prone to think that hospitals are philanthropic or charitable institutions. There is a crippling shortage at the present time, and we must not ignore the needs of our citizens.
Before I enter into a discussion of health problems, there is another matter closely allied with the question of health, and which was discussed by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) in his speech in this debate as reported at page 218 of Hansard. He was referring to refugee doctors. On behalf of the medical profession of Canada, may I say that I strongly resent the speech he made in Toronto, a report of which appeared in the Ottawa Journal of January 31 last. He is quoted as saying:
The Canadian medical profession has actively worked to discourage the entry of refugee doctors into Canada.
The same type of statement was made by Dr. Keenleyside, the deputy minister of mines and resources, and it was repeated in an article in Maclean's magazine of February 1. Dr. Keenleyside said:
The only trade union that has been adamant in its official opposition to the admission of competitive D.P.'s has been the medical profession.
Such a statement is inaccurate, mischievous and misleading. To clarify the situation I intend to present the facts to the house. Severe criticism has been directed towards the medical profession, and there has been considerable controversy over the admission of doctors from central Europe. This has taken the form of a rash of speeches, editorials, and even sermons. There are potent reasons for caution in opening the gates to all who have had some training in dentistry or in medicine.
In Canada and in the United States medical schools are graded by a rigid standard set up by the American medical association. Under this classification the nine Canadian schools at present giving full courses are fully approved and classed A. There are no standards for medical schools in Europe. A graduate from Europe may be from a good school or he may be from a school that is completely unknown to the licensing bodies in Canada. Some of them are known to have very low standards. Some of the European schools, which were of a high standard a generation or two ago, have fallen far below the standard of our own Canadian universities.

There was a time when Vienna and Berlin [DOT]were important post-graduate centres in medical teaching. In fact, they were a mecca as far as post-graduate training was concerned, but they no longer hold that position. You can understand why that is so apparent. Medical standards in Canada are high. They are probably as high as can be found in any country in the world. We cannot afford to lower our standards with medical imports of low standard, or imports who have been out of practice for so long a period that they are not competent to practise their profession without further training. Public interest does not permit a double standard of qualifications; and all physicians, whether trained in Canada or elsewhere, must measure up to the licensing requirements in effect.
Let me make it clear, Mr. Speaker, that a doctor whose medical degree has been obtained anywhere in the world can establish himself in Canada, provided: first, that he enters the country legally; second, that he obtains an enabling certificate; third, that he passes the examination of the medical council of Canada; and fourth, that he registers this certificate with the provincial licensing body. The statement of the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) that the medical profession is actively working to discourage the entry of refugee doctors into Canada is utter nonsense. The Canadian medical association is not uncharitable or unkindly toward these members of the profession who are in such a sorry plight. They are glad and happy to render any assistance in their power. The matter of competition is not a factor. The public should be informed that medical acts are designed not to protect the doctors but solely to protect the public. There are in Canada areas that are medically overpopulated, as well as those medically underpopulated; but I would point out that of the sixty refugee doctors who came into this country in 1947 and were licensed, only five have taken up practice in rural areas. It has been suggested that refugee doctors be admitted on the understanding that they must reside in country districts. Canada has never compelled any of her new citizens to live in any circumscribed areas; and there would be a hue and cry if the authorities should devise regulations compelling any doctors to live in the country if they wished to live elsewhere. We do need doctors in certain rural areas; but the fact is that doctors are not there now because of the conditions of practice and the question of remuneration.

When we consider some of the other countries of the world we discover these facts. Ethiopia, a country of 12 million persons, reported at the close of the war that not one native doctor or nurse was left; they had been entirely liquidated by the enemy. Czechoslovakia reported that, of the 12,000 doctors in that country when war began, some sixty per cent or 7,000 were either killed or missing. Now we turn to the Far East. China, with over 400 million people, had less than 12,000 trained doctors. During the war the Chinese army was served by 30,000 medical officers, and of these only seven per cent had any medical training whatever. India with 400 million people reported 40,000 doctors to serve that population. Liberia, with a population of 2,500,000, has only one doctor.
In Canada we are served by 13,000 doctors, which with an estimated population of 13 million gives an average of one doctor per thousand people, an average higher than anywhere else in the world. This number can

The Address-Mr. Blair take care of the medical needs of our country, and can also make allowance for those who come to our shores from time to time from other lands. In addition, the university of Saskatchewan is well on its way to developing a faculty of medicine. Ottawa university has a faculty of medicine, well equipped and with classes which will soon graduate. The university of British Columbia is considering establishing a medical school. There may be some argument about areas that are overpopulated, and it may be said that the distribution might be improved. But it is very apparent that in comparison with the rest of the world Canada is reasonably well off for doctors. I would draw attention also to the fact that a large number of young veterans of the last war who came back and started in medicine will be graduating from our schools in the next year or two. So it might be well for people whose statements show they are totally unacquainted with the facts to become fully conversant with such matters before making inaccurate public utterances.
Now, sir, I come back to the matter under discussion when I entered this debate. When I came into this house a week ago Wednesday, the day of the speech by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), I could see that something unusual was going to happen here. I wondered what it was all about. Perchance it was some grave international incident or something of that kind. The press had copies of papers and were going over them; the galleries were full; the diplomatic gallery was filled with officials of the Department of National Health and Welfare. Then I realized just what was going to happen. Finally the minister came upon the scene; he was the principal actor, and he rose to speak on the health grants which were introduced last spring. From his description of those grants I gained the impression, which I think was general, that they were a personal gift from the minister or from a beneficent government. Sir, we of this party believe that this or any other government is justified in spending money on public health. Let there be no argument about it. We do reserve the right, however, to criticize the administration when we feel the money is not being spent to the advantage of the Canadian taxpayer.
I listened with interest, sir, but with a growing sense of resentment as the speech proceeded. The minister was very confident about himself. During this speech he exhibited-and I am going to talk plainly to him-a manner of braggadocio not in keeping with the ideals or traditions of those who throughout the centuries have sought to heal. I remember, sir, the wonderful

accomplishments of the provinces when they were working with their own resources in the field of health. I remember the sacrifices made by physicians and surgeons, nurses, men and women who have devoted their lives to healing and the elimination of misery. I remember the work of those other voluntary agencies which have been responsible for so much good in the field of health during the past years. The ethics of the medical profession and those who are associated with them in the art of healing have never permitted advertising. Throughout the whole speech the minister did not hesitate to use the pronouns "I" and "we" when referring to his work and that of the officials of his department. I might point out to the minister that he has only held this position for two years. His whole speech showed a misconception of the picture of health in Canada, and especially of the other agencies which have been responsible in the past decades for the fight against the inroads of disease, misery and suffering.
On the 30th day of June last year, in the dying hours of the session when everyone was tired, hot and anxious to get home, I dealt at length with these grants. It will be impossible to cover them today, but I am going to touch on one or two. First, the grant for crippled children is praiseworthy. But, in view of the fact this grant only amounts to $500,000 for the nine provinces, I should say it seems to be a small amount when compared with the expenditures of the provinces at the present time. The various service organizations have supported the provincial effort. If the best possible results are to be obtained, I believe credit should go where credit is due.
I am familiar with the background of the promotion and financing of a crippled children's camp, "Merrywood on the Rideau", in my constituency of Lanark. I happen to know that this camp was substantially financed by Rotary clubs as well as by a grant from the province of Ontario. From my knowledge of the money that has been spent on this one small project, the grant given to the provinces by the federal government for this purpose is entirely inadequate.
I now come to the question of arthritis. It is an old question and one that has been discussed in this house very often.

Yes, very important. I cannot find myself in agreement with the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) in his approach to the subject. During the past year the public press has contained many reports concerning a recently formed Cana-

dian arthritis and rheumatism society. There are many inaccuracies in these reports. Before further discussion of this society I shall give you something of the history of it.
The Canadian rheumatism association, which is a counterpart of the American rheumatism association, had always met annually along with the Canadian medical association. The exception to this rule was during the war years. This society was a branch of the Canadian medical association. In 1947 the meeting of this association was held at Sunnybrook hospital, Toronto. In that year the Canadian medical association met at Winnipeg. There were nine members present and they were informed by the president of the association that the dominion was sponsoring a new arthritis society and that the Canadian rheumatism association had better get in on it. This is the manner in which the government was approached by the Canadian rheumatism association.
At the next annual meeting of the Canadian rheumatism association in June 1948, the fact that the new Canadian arthritis and rheumatism society had been organized was not even brought up for discussion. The organization meeting of the new Canadian arthritis and rheumatism society was held in Ottawa in 1947 and January of 1948 under the chairmanship of the federal Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin). No preliminary discussions concerning this new national society were held in any open meeting of any medical society in Canada.

The Canadian medical association was represented by the secretary, Dr. T. C. Routley, and one delegate. Most of the doctors present were from governments, the Department of Veterans Affairs, health and research agencies and institutions. Very few general practitioners were present, and they are the ones who come in contact with arthritis. On the official program, three of the four speakers were associated with the Department of Veterans Affairs. There were no elections, and the committees were all appointed. Few of the doctors had any previous training in arthritis work.
The new Canadian arthritis and rheumatism society has existed for thirteen months. To date, there has been no public meeting of the society. It is presumed the original committee is still in charge. There has been no discussion of this society in any open meeting of the Canadian medical association or its provincial branches. The only information that doctors have concerning this new
The Address-Mr. Blair society is what has appeared in the public press and the bulletins of the Department of National Health and Welfare. A combined lay and medical arthritis society had previously been organized in British Columbia and it offered to join forces with the new society.
It has been my opinion that the Minister of National Health and Welfare made a great sacrifice when he entered parliament. In the financial world, as a promoter of stock companies, he would have been a success. His promoting abilities were fully shown when he organized the Canadian arthritis and rheumatism society and printed the first prospectus for his stock. He sold off all the common stock of no par value and retained the preferred shares with promise of interest and profits for himself.
The reports in the public press appearing at infrequent intervals dealing with the new society and its officers make reference almost exclusively to Sunnybrook hospital. It is reported that this hospital now functions as an arthritis centre and has special equipment and new treatments for arthritis. Apparently the press is under the impression that the Department of Veterans Affairs hospitals give courses of instruction for general practitioners. No notices of these courses ever appeared in any of the medical journals of any medical society in Canada. It is well to look into the true situation. The Department of Veterans Affairs doctors have no better training in arthritis work than any other doctors and it is doubtful whether they have any new treatment. It is doubtful whether these hospitals have any new equipment. Other general hospitals have much the same type of equipment. I mention the equipment in the Queen Elizabeth hospital in Toronto, which has one of the two Hubbard tanks in Canada. The Toronto Western Hospital is well equipped, and the patients there receive special attention in an outdoor arthritis clinic. It is doubtful whether there is in Canada any teaching hospital; that is a hospital connected with a hospital school that has an arthritis clinic used for teaching purposes. There are few doctors in Canada who have received any specialized training in the treatment of arthritis.
I have a few suggestions to make as to how this matter could be handled. I am making these suggestions because I have criticized the set-up. I made the suggestions before in this house. The first thing that is essential is a correct diagnosis, and correct treatment in the early stages. This would reduce the number of patients with crippling conditions, and it would decrease the number of hospital beds for chronic cases. There is
29087-73J

The Address-Mr. Blair an immediate need for information and assistance for doctors and especially general practitioners because they are faced with the problem of treating patients with arthritis.
The problem of arthritis should be part of general medicine. These patients are found in all hospitals across the country seeking relief. The matter of specialized treatment is so important that there should be specialized teaching of the care of arthritis in all the medical schools where there are medical students and internes. It should be taught in general hospitals where there are patients of all ages and both sexes. In Sunnybrook there is only one age group, principally male, except a few nurses who are unlucky enough to contract this disease. I have suggested in previous speeches in this house that there is a necessity of refresher courses.
The objectives of the new society, when announced at the organization meetings, were commendable. It is obvious, sir, that the new society was organized in close co-operation with the Department of Veterans Affairs. This leads the average practitioner in Canada to fear that the society, in using D.V.A. doctors, may sponsor a form of state medicine, and they actually are afraid. Health matters, sir, are still under the jurisdiction of the provinces, and state medicine has not yet been adopted in Canada. The problem of arthritis is too big and too far-reaching to be controlled by a small group. It demands the attention of the whole medical profession, and especially the general practitioners who are in touch with it from day to day. It should be discussed with the Canadian and provincial medical associations. Medical schools should be consulted, because it is necessary for them to teach the care of arthritics. A survey of the whole situation should be made, giving the number of patients and the present requirements for attacking the problem. Above all, sir, a stop should be put to this ill-advised publicity which is giving misleading information to the public. To raise false hopes is a cruel type of propaganda. At the present time the propaganda is taking the form of such headlines in the papers as "war on arthritis", "tackling the arthritis problem", and so on. I know where these press reports come from. These are the headlines that we read every once in a while in the papers.
I noted that in the bulletin put out by the Department of National Health and Welfare, volume III, No. 6, March, 1948, there were eight pages devoted to arthritis. That is praiseworthy. I shall tell you something further. Three of the pages in this bulletin show pictures of Sunnybrook hospital. That 
is the only place in which they have seen arthritis that they know anything about. That is the impression they give. Before statements are given to the people with a build-up such as "war on arthritis" it would be well to remember that there are six hundred thousand people across Canada, of whom one hundred and twenty-five thousand are crippled in bed or in wheel chairs, who are looking for relief from this terrible condition. They are begging for something to be done now.
We have had a lot of propaganda so far but we have had very little action. Mention has been made several times in this debate of a national health plan, and something was said about it in the speech from the throne. It is discussed and glibly talked about. The Prime Minister talked about it when he introduced the health grants last May. He made a statement which will be found on page 3935 of Hansard. One hon. member on this side of the house quoted it the other day. He told us what these expenditures would mean in the preservation of health and the saving of human life, to say nothing of the lessening of human suffering and misery, and not infrequently despair. He told us it was beyond calculation. No hon. member in this house could disagree with that; no hon. member could say that it is not true of any sums spent for health reasons; but I point out to you, Mr. Speaker, that these conditions have been waiting for thirty years before the party which forms this government took any action. It was on their program in 1919. It would be difficult to estimate the casualties which have occurred and the misery endured during those thirty years before the Liberal party made any attempt to deal with this situation.
At the time of the introduction of the health grants in May 1948 a full debate was promised. That debate was left to the last day of the session. The minister kept promising all through last session that we would have a chance to debate this matter. At two o'clock on the afternoon of the last day of the session we got a chance to say something about it. We approved these grants; we approved grants to raise the health standard in Canada; that is, we approved the spending of the money to raise health conditions in Canada, and we voted for them gladly.
This party has long realized the necessity for a plan of health in the Dominion of Canada. Let there be no doubt where this party stands on that now. We stand in favour of a plan which, in co-operation with the provinces, will give the people the maximum of services, and yet be a plan of freedom, where the doctors will not be civil ser-

vants, and which will allow free choice between doctor and patient. We have got a full realization of the deficiencies in treatment services in Canada and in our preventive services, and we stand ready to implement a plan to overcome these deficiencies, and which will raise health standards in Canada to the equal of that in any other country of the world.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset I wish
to express my congratulations to the new members of the cabinet:	the former prime
minister of Manitoba (Mr. Garson), the former Under-Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) and the young minister of reconstruction (Mr. Winters). Their experience and their brilliant qualities, applied to the service of Canada, will surely give very good results.
I now want to say a word about the leader of the opposition and member for Carleton (Mr. Drew); he has been outstanding in several ways, some more or less brilliant than others. He succeeds a long line of leaders of the opposition. The seat of the leader of the opposition has been in unstable equilibrium these last few years. I therefore wish him success in his career and I trust the members of his party will make his reign as leader of the opposition long and agreeable and on behalf of the Liberals I can assure him of our fullest co-operation.
I wish every success to the member for Nicolet-Yamaska. I have known him personally for many years and our relations have always been most friendly. His integrity in the practice of his profession, the devotion with which he discharges his duties as protonotary, will certainly be of use to him in the exercise of his mandate. I know what principles he expounded during his election campaign; I believe he will soon realize that he has come to the wrong parliament and that the man who is today foisting his leadership upon him is merely Dr. Jekyll's Mr. Hyde.
I also congratulate the new member for Laval-Two Mountains (Mr. Demers). His speech on the address has shown that his services will be useful to his party and that the people of his constituency had every right to give him their confidence.
Mr. Speaker, the speech from the throne this year is a complete, constructive and realistic synthesis of each and every one of the problems which are presently troubling the minds of our people as Canadian citizens and citizens of the world. Seldom has a ses-
The Address-Mr. Cournoyer sional statement of government policy been submitted for our consideration with such concision and lucidity, such clearness in presenting the facts and such determination in planning for the future. In short, this document reveals the qualities of logic, sincerity and deep wisdom of the man who personally inspired it in his capacity as adviser to His Excellency, our Prime Minister.
Under these circumstances, as a member of this house, I share the hopes of our people. Like so many Canadians, I was labouring under the illusion that the Conservative party, having a new leader, would carry out constructively its task of criticizing the government's policies and shed about that amount of light which our democracy has a right to expect from the official opposition, whose duty it is to co-operate in the good management of the country.
To me and to all Canadians that was a sad disappointment.
So far, we have seen the leader of the opposition delve into his own past for the sole purpose of disowning it. We have seen him rummage about for old speeches. We have seen him endeavour, quite clumsily at times, to resuscitate past problems and demand solutions for matters settled long ago.
Provincial autonomy is his main theme. On that note the leader of the opposition sings, as Roosevelt would have said, from both sides of his mouth. He demands autonomy with a great show of eloquence, but when he was the leader of his party in Ontario, he was demanding the abolition of provincial governments.
Another of his themes is communism; he merely amplifies what all people say just as sincerely and with much more practical common sense.
Finally, he refers to a letter dating as far back as 1942 and dealing with the Hong Kong tragedy; he is the only one who has not forgotten all about that letter or perhaps who has read it.
The satisfaction which the leader of the opposition takes in handling his old papers, in reading old letters, could easily be understood if it were but the harmless foible of those who enjoy evoking their past because they no longer have the strength to live their present.
Those are men of another era, and the Canadians will never entrust the destinies of their young nation to a group of mummies, however eloquent the latter may be.
The bold and dynamic policies of the Liberal party, which marches resolutely and fearlessly toward the future, is noticeable throughout the speech from the throne.

Let me point out a few examples, in connection with the Atlantic pact, with the development of our merchant marine and Our shipyards.
If the Progressive Conservatives have thought they could win over the province of Quebec and gain votes through their silence and their equivocal stand on the Atlantic pact, they have made a mistake which can only be expected from tenth-rate politicians.
To think that the French Canadians refuse to take their place among free men who oppose communist slavery is to be greatly misinformed as regards their intelligence, their fundamental vigour and their Christian spirit.
Never perhaps has there been such a degree of unanimity among Canadians of both great races as to the ultimate aims of our international policy. Never has their confidence been greater in their Prime Minister who, taking the lead among the rulers of democratic nations, has sounded the call to all men of good will and issued to the western nations that slogan which the French Canadians know so well: "Let us unite!"
Only the Tories, these men of a bygone century, still think they can wave the old bugaboos to reap votes in the province of Quebec. Quebec considers these vulgar tactics as an insult. Just as the people of Quebec opposed imperialistic wars where they considered that Canada's interests were not at stake, so today they join with enthusiasm the movement of free humanity to save peace without neglecting justice, and to maintain Christian values, which are so deeply Canadian, even if this entails preparing for war.
It seems to me, however, that we attach too much importance to the purely military aspect of the Atlantic pact. In a radio speech the Prime Minister gave the democratic alliance an economic and cultural meaning which corresponds to the pacifist sentiment of our people as well as to the new needs of our national economy.
The constitutional evolution of Canada, the crumbling of the former world order have shattered the framework of the British empire; in other words the framework within which were formerly brought into play our economic, cultural and international relations with other countries is now disappearing.
India and Pakistan are precariously accepting dominion status; Burma is no longer a colony; Ireland becomes a republic; South Africa is subjected to a nationalistic storm; even Newfoundland, that old colony,


is severing its ties with the mother country to become the tenth province of Canada.
In addition to these geographical disturbances, there are the monetary struggles, the conflict in currency and the dollar situation. Our imperial trade routes in the sterling area threaten to close up. Thanks to the tremendous efforts of the Liberal government, they are still open to the greatest advantage of our farmers and manufacturers. The very framework of the British empire is crumbling, according to some people. So much the better, will say all true Canadians who consider that their young nation was cramped and paralysed in this association which was too seclusive and too much dominated by its sister, and equal, Great Britain. Let us now replace this old order by a new order. Let us replace the free association of British nations with a larger association of free men from all races. Amongst this enlarged commonwealth, amongst this alliance, which would not be imperial but human in character, Canada would play, unrestricted, her part as an adult nation, respected throughout the world because she aims only at promoting the ideals of peace, and has no other imperialistic designs than that of expanding the domain of human happiness.
The economic and cultural alliance brought about by the Atlantic pact does not stop at promoting Canada's peace-loving dreams and humane ideals. It can become the framework of our own national economy which depends on our export trade to such a fantastic extent. Our Prime Minister has said that it will take more than the pooling of our armed forces to bring peace to the world.
Canadians keep close watch on those world markets that spell for them prosperity or unemployment. More particularly have my constituents in Richelieu-Vercheres-shipbuilders, sailors, farmers, dealers-grasped the real economic significance of our international problems. They are peace-loving people, but they are determined that their stamp of manhood and their Christian faith shall survive.
They are also realistic and patriotic. That is why they rejoice over the fact that Canada is no longer bound by a too narrow imperial framework, and put their trust in the new economic, social, and cultural order pledged by the Atlantic pact.
The signing of the Atlantic pact will contribute not only to the peace for which we are all yearning, not only to our material well-being, but also to the development of our navy and our shipyards.

I represent the constituency of Richelieu-Vercheres, where are located the most important shipyards in the country. Those yards have been developed and improved during the war, as a result of the Liberal government's policy. I wish to take this opportunity to pay a tribute to the workers of my village, of the town of Sorel and of the whole district. Their industry, their technical knowledge, their ability and especially their willingness to co-operate, have permitted the employers' spirit of enterprise to make an admirable contribution to the creation of a Canadian navy and to the victory of the allied forces.
As a matter of fact, at the very beginning of the conflict in 1939, Canada only had 35 ships with a combined capacity of about
240,000	tons. These vessels were left-overs from world war I. My older compatriots remember seeing the few shipyards of that time close their doors one after the other. This almost complete shut-down of the shipbuilding industry, during the whole period between the two wars, explains why our navy had so few units in 1939.
But during the war our shipyards, especially that of St. Joseph de Sorel, were so extensively developed that in 1946 our navy included 448 merchant vessels of various tonnages without mentioning the corvettes, mine sweepers, tow-boats and invasion barges. These figures indicate the productive capacity of our shipyards.
The vessels were placed at the disposal of Canadian companies. Unfortunately the latter are experiencing certain difficulties. I trust that the Canadian maritime commission which was established on November 6, 1947, due to the initiative of the genial Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier), will soon suggest the necessary steps to be taken in order to ensure the survival of our marine industry.
Section 6 of the act creating it provides that the commission shall recommend to the minister such policies and measures as it considers necessary for the operation, maintenance, manning and development of a merchant marine and a shipbuilding and ship-repairing industry commensurate with Canadian maritime needs.
The task of the commission is not as simple as it looks on the face of it for, although our prosperity rests fundamentally on our trade, our Canadian merchant marine and our shipbuilding industry have not been sufficiently encouraged in the past to compete with others. The minister has pointed out the difficulties himself.
The Address-Mr. Cournoyer
Practically all countries whose ships ply the seas have enacted rigid laws to control coastal navigation, that is to say, water transport of goods within their borders. Since 1789 in the United States and since 1793 in France, to mention but those two countries, ships of foreign registry are not allowed to transport goods between two ports within their respective boundaries. These countries have reserved for themselves their boats, their seamen, their waterways and their coasts. In Canada, not only does the British navy enjoy the same privileges as the Canadian navy, but in addition, ships of other countries may carry on coastwise trade on our shores, subject to the maritime commission's permission.
Until the provisions of the shipping act are made more rigid for all boats not built in Canada, and until the provisions of subsection (i) of section 12 of the 1930 imperial conference's report are acted upon, I do not think our navy will be able to survive. The trade between two points in Canada should be restricted to ships registered in Canada and manned by Canadian seamen.
I shall support this statement with a striking example. Hon. members know that Sorel is about to become one of the great steel producing centres in Canada. The titanium ore treated there comes from Havre St. Pierre and not from Ungava as many are led to believe. It means that millions of tons of ore would be shipped from Havre St. Pierre for treatment in the Sorel plants. The American company which will operate this plant will surely need ships to transport this material. But not a single Canadian company will be able to compete with foreign shipowners, the British or Norwegian companies, for example.
True, in England ships can be built for less, because of lower labour costs and different working conditions. Moreover, the operation of a Canadian ship costs $680 per day, while that of an English ship only amounts to $460 per day. Under such conditions no Canadian operator can tender with any hope of success.
If we let commonwealth and foreign ships compete with Canadian ships in coastal trade, we can easily see what will happen. The hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Langlois) who spoke of this matter last year, as reported on page 4150 of Hansard for 1948, said, and I quote:
The least we could do would be to charge duty on ships built outside Canada. Only by legislation

The Address-Mr. Cournoyer reserving coastal trade to our own ships and levying duties on foreign-built ships will Canada promote the organization and maintenance of a Canadian merchant navy and at the same time establish in our country a sound and prosperous shipbuilding industry.
If it is to survive, our merchant marine must be protected by legislation. Because of the type of labour to whom they provide employment and a means of livelihood, shipyards need state assistance.
It should be recalled that during the war, the shipbuilding industry, apart from subsidiary concerns, employed as many as 53,000 men and, last year, still kept 16,000 on the pay roll.
Regulations dealing with our coastal trade should be a boon to sailors, operators, workers and shipbuilders. It is not a matter of sentiment but a case of survival.
Realizing the full import of this problem, the Liberal delegates meeting at the party convention held in Ottawa in August, 1948, passed the following resolution:
1.	The Liberal party is in favour of supporting the efforts of the Canadian maritime commission to strengthen the Canadian merchant marine and to protect it against any foreign competition in Canadian waters.
2.	The necessary amendments to the Canada Shipping Act, 1934, to establish a separate registration system for Canadian ships.
I hope the day is not far off when the people of my constituency will see a Canadian merchant marine, proudly flying a Canadian flag, sail the majestic St. Lawrence and the seven seas.
The present government has brought about great achievements in the field of the shipping industry, for which the people will be grateful.
On behalf of my constituents, I wish to thank the government for having allowed the continuation of shipbuilding at St. Joseph de Sorel, where the Marine Industries' shipyards, a concern which is a credit to our province and to Canada, are located.
At the end of the war, we were worried. Our population had considerably increased as a result of the opening of the Sorel Industries' and Marine Industries' shipyards. Thanks to the millions of dollars lent France by the present government, our men have been able to work since the end of the war with the same spirit and the same devotion they showed during the war for an equally noble cause.

These ships are finished, the yards are almost closed, but once again the government helped us, and, through the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton), the shipyards of my constituency and its workers got an order for a new icebreaker. Unfortunately, due to circumstances over which the government-or for that matter, anybody-has no control, construction has not started on this project. I hope that before long the people of Sorel and of the surrounding district will forget the hard times and worry they have known throughout this winter.
I also wish to thank the present Minister of Transport. If the Sorel Industries concern, which produced so much ordnance, is still in operation today, it is because of the contracts received from the Canadian National Railways. Those splendid workshops are now repairing used railway cars, but I am sure it could build new ones. I earnestly request the minister to take this request under consideration.
There would be much to say about government policies since the war. The Liberal party is not perfect; it is a human institution. But it must be admitted that, in every field of Canada's political activity, much has been achieved in the general interest of the public.
If the senior member of this house, the distinguished member for Glengarry (Mr. Mackenzie King) was prime minister of his country longer than any other man in the world, it is because his economic and social policies were considered best for the people.
At the beginning of my remarks, I referred to the difficulties encountered by the world in its search for a new order. The people of Canada are seeking a new social and economic order just as the world is also seeking a new order.
This is where the matter of taxes comes in. Taxes are high; they must be lowered. As a matter of fact, the real hardships caused the taxpayer by the high level of taxation are enlarged and magnified by irresponsible politicians who, for electoral purposes, strive by every possible means to induce among the people a psychosis of resentment and discontent.
Nobody likes taxes. To ask for their reduction requires neither imagination nor heroism, as everybody favours this theory. But I maintain that the Progressive Conservative party should be the last to blame the

government in this respect. Indeed, if that party had been in power during the war, we would be paying three times as many taxes, and I shall prove it.
The house will recall that during the war they were never satisfied with the Canadian effort. Billion dollar expenditures on behalf of Great Britain were too scarce; army estimates were never high enough and Canadian fighters always too few in number. They blackmailed the government by pitting the other provinces against Quebec. Had their advice been followed, full conscription would have been in effect at the beginning of the war. In short, expense was never too high. Moreover, after Germany's defeat, they began clamouring for conscription to fight Japan. That is why there were no Progressive Conservative candidates in Quebec for the 1945 election.

Besides, this taxation situation is not peculiar to Canada. While all nations of the

The Address-Mr. Cournoyer world are being taxed more heavily than we are, while nearly all foreign governments have increased their taxes, the Canadian government was able to manage the affairs of this country and reduce taxes on three different occasions.
Mr. Truman has just increased the taxes in the United States. Mr. Dewey, the up and coming man during the last election for the presidency of the United States, is fighting against his own supporters, in the New York legislature, for an increase in taxation. The provincial government, just recently approved by the electors, raised the sales tax by 1 per cent. It took over the 3 cent gasoline tax that the Ottawa people had just surrendered; it again prescribes a monthly school charge; it raised the corporation taxes; school text books are no longer free.
In Canada, the government has surrendered the 3 cent gasoline tax, duties on estates of less than $50,000, the 25 per cent amusement tax, besides granting three successive tax abatements. In addition the government refunded, with interest, approximately $240 million, last year, and $270 million this year, of compulsory savings.
Well, notwithstanding what goes on in the world, we have every reason to believe-and I hope for it and ask for it eagerly-that the government will reduce taxes, thanks to their good administration, without giving up their social security program but by getting the money necessary for its application from those who possess the largest share of the wealth of the nation.
The Liberal party, under the guidance of the Prime Minister (Mr. Louis St. Laurent), that great Canadian of whom we are proud, will direct our country in the difficult search for a new world order through our alliance with the democratic nations, and for [DOT] a new social order through justice for all social classes in Canada. On problems as important as that of our merchant marine, they will apply the solution of the national interests of Canada, and their internationalism will always be enlightened by the nationalist care of a young nation with faith in its future.
