Before proceeding with my main subject, I should like to make some comments in a humble way on the remarks that were made by the member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid). We listened to scorn and a certain amount of sarcasm being heaped upon the head of the member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Argue) earlier in the afternoon. Apparently he had made an error in calculation on the matter of the eleven months or less than eleven months that had elapsed since the government health program went into effect. The comparison was made that a six year old child would know better. I remember that only a few days ago the member for New Westminster, in answer to a suggestion from this side of the house that smaller chocolate bars were a way of gypping the youngsters of Canada, made the statement that smaller chocolate bars were healthier and, said he, "I venture to say I can prove that it is a fact." A fact is a very important thing. As the member for New Westminster said this afternoon, facts are chiels that winna ding. My pronunciation of the dialect is not as good as his because I am two generations removed from the old sod, but nevertheless I, too, would venture to remark that chiels are facts that winna ding, and that the children who listen to his statement are bound to misinterpret it, to say the least. They will not think of the hon. member in a very kindly way. If they had been able to vote for him I am afraid they would be likely to vote against him in the coming general election.
The reproach was made that we on this side of the house are in favour of better old age pensions, that we want to look after the incurables, and that we want to take care of a certain number of veterans who are not very well cared for at the present time, and that at the same time we are in favour of a reduction of taxation. The comment was made that that seemed to be contradictory. Let me say that we think that exemptions of $750 for a single person and $1,500 for a married person are much too small. The exemptions should be much higher than that because of present high prices, and because of conditions in the country. At the same time we do not feel that if our policies were carried out it would necessarily mean a cut in social services, limited as they are, or that it would prevent the improvement of existing

social services. We propose to cut taxes at the end where taxation is hurting the most people, who can least afford to pay, and increase taxation amongst that small section of the population which has the most money and can most afford to pay. It seems to me that it is reasonable, that it is logical, that it is humanitarian, and that it is plain common sense.
The suggestion has been made in this house, and it was made again this afternoon, that one of the causes of communism is the lack of social services, and that if social services were improved we would have less to fear from the growth of communism. I do not deny that statement but I would suggest that we in the C.C.F. group have advocated that social services should be extended to those countless thousands who need them, and need them desperately, not because we are afraid of communism but because we think it is the decent, humane thing to do. Psychologically that seems to me to be a much worthier reason, and I would suggest that it is the point of view that should be adopted by the government in relation to the problem.
In the days of the depression it used to be a common saying amongst our people that the poor get poorer and the rich get richer. But the days of the depression have gone, we have come through a war, and we have been in the piping times of peace for the last five years. During that period the poor have still got poorer and the government has got richer. The poorest amongst the poor are the old age pensioners, and every time they pay for food, shelter and clothing they pay a part of that taxation which has accumulated to the point where we expect a surplus of at least $500 million, and we have had larger surpluses annually for the past two or three years.
When the government come to us and say that they are engaged in cyclical budgeting, and that they want to save during the fat years in order to take care of the lean, I say to them that paying off the national debt is an excellent piece of business and it is good law, but they should remember their fathers and their mothers before they remember the bondholders. I believe in the statement in the good book: remember thy father and thy mother that thy days may be long in the land that the Lord thy God has given thee. I believe that is true today, and that it is a better rule than remembering the bondholders and paying off the national debt. I believe that any surplus should go where it is so urgently needed.
In this debate I have listened to members of the Conservative party, the Liberal party, the Social Credit party and the C.C.F. All have agreed that something should be done for the old age pensioners; and I believe that

year after year, if asked this question, they would be so agreed. Yet nothing comparable to what is necessary has been done to date. However, we are looking forward with the thought that a general election is in the air. We hope the government, with the sort of generosity that is always shown before a general election, will move in the interests of these old people who have spent their lives building up our country, who have made it possible for us to enjoy what we are enjoying today, and who at this late stage of their lives should be given some ease and comfort and some security in their declining years.
I want to deal also with the matter of superannuated civil servants. When asked why something cannot be done for these people the reason is always advanced that superannuated civil servants are paid out of a fund that is on an actuarial basis. Of course, to some of us who understand insurance and know what an actuarial basis means, this may sound very logical. But to the individual who is trying to live on $40 a month, all this talk does not mean very much. Financially it may be the correct thing; but from the point of view of the human being, he neither understands it nor will he tolerate it. We employed these people in the service of the state in various activities, whether humble or important. They - gave years of service to our nation, and we are an honest people who wish to pay our debts. We will not lightly forgive a government which permits the superannuated civil servants of the country, in their grey hairs, to suffer as these people are suffering today; and I say that, despite actuarial bases or any other kind of financial excuse for not coming through with what is absolutely necessary for our retired civil servants.
In the course of my remarks I should like to deal with the situation that has developed in my city of Vancouver. Out there our people have returned to the period of the depression. It is as though the years in between have vanished; the piping times of peace, when we enjoyed high wages, full employment and full pockets have gone, and we are back in the days of the soup line. I have newspaper pictures here showing men lined up at a long table, and the headline is, "Soup kitchen business brisk." The writer goes on to say;
"Soup kitchens" are operating in Vancouver to fill the stomachs of hungry men who have exhausted their unemployment insurance benefits or are not eligible for any. Shavei ar tl unshaven, clean and unkempt, with the haggard look that comes from weeks of desperation, hundreds of forlorn men haunt the premises where social agencies ladle soup by the bowl or hand out meal tickets.
Now in my province they run to over fifty thousand, many of whom are not eligible for unemployment insurance or who have 29087-74J
The Address-Mr. Young exhausted their eligibility and have no means of maintenance. I have here a news report which should interest the house, because it quotes the chief of the community chest, a very responsible person chosen from other responsible people in our society, who is capable and willing, and who has the leisure and possibly the security to interest himself in carrying on where government social security ends and where the need is still felt. In his speech, which is reported in the Vancouver Sun of March 1, he says:
The retiring president said at the chest's annual meeting Monday night that "hungry and cold people get a bit impatient when they wait on the enactment of statutes." He said both single and family men have used up their unemployment insurance benefits and have no income. The matter must not be "smugly smoothed over" for another year, he said.
This is not an impatient C.C.F.'er, but the head of the community chest in Vancouver.
In my constituency we have one of the most beautiful natural parks in Canada. It is known from coast to coast and all over the continent. Wherever you hear tell of tourist paradises, you hear mention of Stanley park in Vancouver. It is an area which was left for our leisure, for our enjoyment; and before I left Vancouver I walked through that park, which is close to my home. Sitting on the benches in the bitter wind were the unemployed men, homeless and foodless. Under their clothes were stuck newspapers to keep out the wind. That is the sort of thing that is transpiring.

Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to be interrupted by the hon. member at length, though I do not mind the odd interruption. I should like to go on and say that the Canadian society of incurables has sent most hon. members, perhaps all of them, a letter setting out their case, part of which

The Address-Mr. Young I am going to present to the house because I believe it is worth listening to. They say:
We cannot forget that thirty years have elapsed and the cycle of Mr. Mackenzie King's premiership has been completed since the desperate need of our Canadian incurables was first presented to our federal government. Members of parliament are still agreeing whole-heartedly that something should be done for them and yet nothing is being done.
And a little further on:
Much has been said about an over-all security plan. That sounds reasonable if it could be brought into immediate existence. We are told that it cannot be done, and in the meantime our incurables are existing shamefully or else dying in poverty.
Then the letter concludes:
We do not believe that the social and economic security of our incurables depends upon a proper relationship between our provincial and federal governments. That excuse will not pacify us any longer. If that were so, right thinking men would have remedied that difficulty before this. We believe that if the federal government so desires they can see that every incurable in Canada is receiving a proper pension of at least seventy-five dollars or more before this session is over. We believe that you do want to, otherwise life is not worth living for the thousands of people for which you are directly responsible clear across Canada.
I have had a great many letters similar to this, but if I were to present them all I would not have time to speak on any other subject. So I am going to present just one other letter dealing with this matter of the necessary social services for which this nation has looked to our present government over the years, as they are related to the $500 million the government is sitting on for the future, and which possibly they used to reduce our national debt last year. Here is a resolution from the Canadian non-pensioned veterans' widows, of which I shall read only part: that all non-pensioned veterans' widows whose late husbands served in any of His Majesty's forces during the great war, 1914-18, be considered under the War Veterans' Allowance Act, whether said husband served in an actual theatre of war or otherwise.
We appeal to the dominion government for the necessity of making prompt provision for the non-pensioned widows of imperial veterans, by the extension of the War Veterans' Allowance Act under the same conditions as the Canadian non-pensioned widow, providing that such widows have been domiciled in the Dominion of Canada for a reasonable time. For example, -
This is a good example, I think.
-the immigrant who has resided not less than a period of three years, can apply for the family allowance; we would urge that the imperial veterans' widows have the same privilege when applying for allowance.
It seems to me that what I have read is reasonable. It comes not from people who, if we support them, will reach a stage where they will not want to support themselves. These people cannot support themselves. These people are a crying shame to our country and to our civilization. It is a shame 
that a land such as Canada, one of the wealthiest in the world, rich in natural resources, despite its enormous wealth and with only twelve million people as compared with Great Britain which has forty-eight million people in that tight little island, is unable to inaugurate a social security program.
On a previous occasion the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) said that some of these social services enjoyed by the British people were instituted by a Liberal government. More honour to the Liberals of Great Britain and less honour to the Liberals of Canada. The final touches were put to the program the British people now enjoy by a parliament just as we have here. If I stood up in that parliament and looked around, however, I would not be able to say to myself, as I am able to do here, every fourth man I see is an honoured and learned member: almost every third member is a member of the legal profession. In the British House of Commons I could look around and see bricklayers, ditch diggers, coal miners and sailors; I could see the representatives of a democratic people and they would represent every form of energy devoted to the interests of humanity, whether it be the energy of the brain or the energy of the muscles. I look forward, Mr. Speaker, to seeing that happen in this house. The reason I look forward to it is that the needs of the people have not been met.
In deciding what is going to happen in our country in the next few months, Mr. Speaker, it would be well to look at the history of elections in Canada since confederation. It is a notable fact that, before any party has taken office federally, that party has been in office in a majority of the provinces. The sole exception to this rule was the last election, which was a victory election. When the party in power federally has lost office in a majority of the provinces, then it has gone down to defeat at the next election. An examination of the political situation in Canada today shows that the Liberal party is no longer in office in a majority of the provinces. If the political rules that have developed in this country have any validity, then this government is like Belshazzar at the feast. It sits sated before the political tables from which it has eaten so long and the handwriting is on the wall, "Mene, mene, tekel, upharsin."-You have been weighed in the balance and found wanting; your kingdom will be divided amongst your enemies.
I say to the government, that is about to happen. On the other hand, I look at the official opposition. I look at them in the early afternoon when they are all in the house. I

see men who have been out in the political wilderness for many years. I find that the average age of that group is probably much higher than the average age of the house as a whole. I find that they look extremely senatorial and dignified. Had the Conservative party been in office, it is quite possible some of them would have occupied seats in that other place ere now. I watch them and see that they have a hungry eye when they look at the front benches on the government side. During the war years they were the greatest patriots. Amongst that group there are two holders of the Victoria Cross. These are the gentlemen who called for an all-out effort during the war and called for conscription. They said "Everything for our country." Today, with those hungry eyes fastened on the government front benches, they are in an alliance with Duplessis. Men are working for them in the elections who, only a few years ago, the Conservatives cried out should be in jail. At that time they said these men were opposed to patriotism-traitors to our country. But today they have compromised, and what a compromise!	_
I say that the people of this country have no choice between the official opposition and the government. It is impossible for a group to straddle the fence as the official opposition proposes to do. When the records of the debates in this house are examined it will be found that the official opposition has not brought up the economic conditions of the immediate future or the problems that face the country from the point of view of bread and butter. They have dillied and dallied with the ancient history of our country and the more recent history of our country in the form of dominion-provincial relations. Worse than that, they propose to bring up the story of Hong Kong. I would say this, Mr. Speaker, that the men and women who survived but who lost brothers and sons in the Hong Kong disaster have suffered enough. To bring this up now in order to make political capital out of it is a stab in the back to the people of Canada. The object of this move is headline hunting. I say that the people of Canada will not thank the Progressive Conservative party for it and will make that fact known at the next election.
In my constituency, Mr. Speaker, we have fine homes and beautiful gardens. As I said before, we have one of the great parks of Canada. There is also the business section and, in the eastern section, there is a slum quarter. As the member for that constituency, I have frequented that quarter, I have called upon these people and discussed their problems with them. I have examined the record and found that, when that area pays rates to the city of Vancouver, the city of Van-
The Address-Mr. Young couver has to pay back additional money to that area in the form of the cost of juvenile delinquency; in the cost of crime; in the form of providing policemen; in the cost of hospitalization for the various social diseases; in the cost of tubercular prevalence; in the cost of infant mortality. All of these things cost more than the city receives from that area. I say this, Mr. Speaker, that the time has come when we in this country are getting into the plight of the people in Europe, we are developing slum dwellers.
I believe that the children of our country should live normal, natural lives. I believe that every child in an ideal society, such as that for which I hope we are struggling-and I include every member in this house- would rise at dawn and sleep at dusk. It would run in the grass. It would stand in the streams in its bare feet, and standing on the round stones it would feel the water rippling and enjoy the sunshine. It would be able to smell the grass, and it would be able to take part in the natural earthbound existence which the natural person has. The children in the slums in my area are cut off from that. They are cut off from anything normal and natural. When they grow up they are foredoomed. Society is against them. Many of them go into the criminal courts. They appear in those courts as pleaders, as vagrants and as criminals. They are there on petty crimes which are always prevalent in an area where an individual has no chance. I believe in equality in a real sense. I believe in equality of opportunity. I believe that everyone in this country has the right to a break, when they are small, anyway. They will all grow up differently. We are all built differently. But if they are given an even break we shall have a better Canada and it will be a more worth-while Canada.
We who sit in this house have these responsibilities, Mr. Speaker, and after we leave this house, nothing that we do or say in the way of an explanation as to how this could not be afforded and that could not be done will redeem that. We ourselves will be responsible, when we go before the people, more for what we have failed to do than for what we have done. And especially responsible will be this Liberal government, and the hon. members who sit on the back benches will be just as responsible as the hon. members who sit on the front benches, because no government survives without the support of all its members.
I do not want to dwell too much on this, but I do want to point out that a special committee on housing was set up by this house fourteen years ago. That committee on

The Address-Mr. Young housing brought in a report which reads in part as follows-I shall read section 4 first:
The formation, institution and pursuit of a policy of adequate housing should be accepted as a social responsibility.
Section 5 reads as follows:
There is no apparent prospect of the low-rental housing need being met through unaided private enterprise building for profit.
Section 13:
The slum areas which have been shown to cast very heavy expenses on many branches of public administration such as health, welfare, fire prevention, administration of justice, et cetera, may justify public assistance, which is likely to prove as sound financially as it is certainly desirable socially.
Therefore all the remarks I have made on slum conditions, all the reasons that I propose to urge on this house for low-rental subsidized housing, were made fourteen years ago by a committee of this house, and yet where are we today? We still have not got it.
There was a report in the newspapers dealing with some of the figures of the experiments which have been made in subsidized housing in the United States. In San Francisco some of the most significant figures came to light. The revenue and expenditures situation in the slum area compared with an equal non-slum area were as follows: Revenues from the non-slum area were $555,600. From a slum area of equivalent size the revenues were $368,000. But the expenditures in the non-slum area were only $86,000 and in the slum area they were $741,000. I have not time to give a breakdown of these figures although I have them here.
May I say this, especially to the Prime Minister, whose published statements in the press of late have shown some slight departure from his original statement made, I believe, some time ago in which he implied ;hat he would not be himself a member of a government that went into the housing business. His more recent statements tend to show that there is a possibility that there is something in this need of people being housed, which is a responsibility of the government.

Mr. Speaker, I should like in the few remaining minutes of my time to refer to the matter brought up yesterday by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier). He referred to the sale of Canadian ships to foreign flags, the reduction of our merchant marine and the consequent unemployment which would follow if- that procedure was very far spread.
I should like to say that the house would expect-and I presume it will receive from the minister concerned-some assurance that Canadian companies are not retaining ownership of shipping and transferring it to foreign flags. Because there is abroad among the sailors on our ships a very definite impression that that has taken place in at least one instance. I have letters on my files to that effect.
We all realize that during the period of the war many young men from Canada went to sea for the first time. They did so in order to help us win the battle of the Atlantic. They had their ships sunk from under them -not once or twice, but sometimes three or four times. Those men have adopted seafaring as a means of making their livelihood, and as their way of life. They received adequate training.
It was suggested that there had been labour trouble in the merchant marine, and that this had an ill effect on the prospects of the industry. Let me say this, that the labour troubles over a period of years have given to our sailors a higher standard of wages and conditions than are to be found in

other merchant navies. The minister himself said that the average wage of a Canadian mariner was $49 higher than that of a British mariner. A Liberal government is liberal, not only in name but, I hope, in its outlook upon the standard of living of the Canadian worker. And it is in the interests of liberalism, as it is in the interests of Canada, that when a standard of living has been achieved no private corporation should be allowed to whittle down that standard of living by hiring cheaper foreign labour. Every effort should be made by the government, when ships are sold, to see to it that pressure is brought to bear to have new keels laid to maintain the standard of labour.

Before taking my seat I should like to draw the attention of the government to the safety regulations on the Vancouver waterfront. May I draw their attention to the fact that for that whole waterfront area at the present time the federal safety inspectors number only two. It
The Address-Mr. Young is the opinion of people who should know, and who are experts in longshoring, that it requires a minimum of six safety inspectors.
The provincial government has jurisdiction over safety regulations, through the workmen's compensation board, as far as the highwater mark. But as the longshoremen in Vancouver work mainly on the ships and on the docks a good deal depends upon the safety regulations being carried out by the federal inspectors. I am given to understand by all sides that the inspectors who are at present engaged on the Vancouver waterfront are doing an excellent job, so far as it is within their power, having due regard to the fact that there are only two of them. It is by no means their fault, individually, that accidents have occurred. However, the rigging used in longshoring is cumbersome in many ways, and if it is to be properly inspected and found to be in good condition we mu?t have a better safety inspection.
I should like to draw attention to the fact that the men who are used for first-aid work are often recruited from among the longshoremen who, after many years of service, have reached an age which is too far advanced for their jobs. That is, they cannot carry out the extremely heavy labour of longshoring. Very often these men are recruited as first-aid men. If they go on the job and a piece of tackle is missing, they are sent back to the yards to pick up that tackle. They may be absent two hours or perhaps a day. If anyone were hurt during their absence no first-aid man would be on the job. In my view the regulations should be more strict respecting the knowledge of first-aid men on the waterfront. I feel this will bear some investigation on the part of the minister concerned.
Then, if I may be permitted, I should like to thank the authorities responsible for the offer of assistance in starting a steel plant in British Columbia. We need a steel plant out there. We have the materials; we have the coal; we have the iron; we have the mines. If it is possible-and I hope it will be-to make financial arrangements whereby the money will be furnished dollar for dollar with the government, it may go a great distance toward relieving the present unemployment situation, and will give us what we need so badly on the west coast, a primary industry to provide employment to thousands of people who come in from other parts of Canada to enjoy our climate, and also people from stricken Europe.
We wish to have a satisfied citizenry, and we also hope that we may not be inflicted with a continuance of the terrible condition of unemployment existing today. In our view

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I at the outset of my remarks extend my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Brown) and the seconder (Mr. Demers) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. These two hon. gentlemen have been given the privilege of taking a leading part in a time-honoured tradition and to them belongs the satisfaction of a job well done. The speech from the throne occupies a real place in our parliamentary system because it provides an opportunity for members of parliament to speak on behalf of the people back home. In the United States they call this traditional speech the speech on the state of the union. In Canada it is the speech from the throne. It is, in fact, a national stocktaking.
In my constituency of Parkdale the cry is for tax relief. The people contend that the income tax and the hidden taxes are getting to be more than they can bear. There is

something wrong with a government which takes from the people a surplus of upwards of $700 million in one year and a surplus of upwards of $600 million the next year. In the army we used to call any additional thing "buckshee." These taxes are buckshee taxes, they are something additional, they represent something that is not needed. The people back home are asking about these buckshee taxes. These taxes have become too heavy and the people are very resentful.
Among these taxes is one that has been referred to a number of times in this house, the tax on soft drinks. A return which I have received shows that in 1946 the revenue from this tax was $17-5 million. In 1947 the amount was even more, and in 1948 it was still higher. This tax has reached the point where the industry is being stifled to some extent. The tax is stopping the people from buying. That means the possibility of unemployment in the industry. I am told by representatives of the industry that if the tax were taken off the saving would all be passed on to the public so that they would be able to buy their soft drinks at the price they paid before the war.
I spoke to the minister about some of these indirect taxes and he gave me to understand that when they got to the point where they were interfering with industry, where there was a likelihood of unemployment, he would have to do something about them. Despite what may have been said by others in this house about this tax, the fact is that this industry is finding the going pretty tough and there will be unemployment if something is not done about the tax.
There is another tax we have not heard so much about, but it is quite important. I refer to the 25 per cent tax on toilet articles and cosmetics which used to be only 10 per cent. In 1941 during the war it was raised to 25 per cent. This tax is getting to the point where it is stifling buying by the public. I know of one United States firm which came here in 1932. They have done a lot of business and employed many people but they are considering seriously giving up because of the results of this tax. It will not be long before you find other companies giving up by reason of the tax. I know another smaller firm in Toronto which finds the going pretty hard for the same reason.
I think all of us want our women folk to look their best and we expect them to purchase cosmetics. They feel resentful over this tax and I submit that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) should reduce it at least to the point where it was in 1941 when it was only ten per cent. Those of us who were overseas during the first great war

remember the comedienne, Elsie Janis, who was the toast of London in those days. She used to sing a song which went something like this: I want a man, a determined man, determined to do what I want him to do. I say to the Minister of Finance that the women of Canada are saying that they want a determined man who will reduce this tax to the point where it was in 1941.
There is also an anomaly in connection with this tax. Shaving cream, hair shampoo, shaving soap and toothpaste are all subject to the 25 per cent tax. I imagine that every one of us uses every day probably those articles upon which we have to pay tax of 25 per cent. They are just ordinary necessities used to cleanse the human body. But toilet soap, another article used to cleanse the body, bears a tax of only five per cent. Why should not this heavy, irritating tax of 25 per cent be reduced, at least to five per cent, so that it would be in line with the toilet soap tax?
I see no reason why necessities like shaving cream, shaving soap, toothpaste and hair shampoo should not be reduced, preferably by taking off all the tax, but in any event to five per cent in line with toilet soap.
I come now to the matter of income tax. Right now people are striving to the limit of their resources to pay this tax, and by the end of the year they have very little to put away for old age and so on. I think we are all finding it increasingly difficult to pay this tax year by year without getting behind. The present exemption of $1,500 for a married man is worth only $750 at the present day value of the dollar, and that is a pretty small exemption. I ask the minister to take cognizance of the platform of the Progressive Conservative party in which we recommend that the exemption be raised to $2,500 for married people and $1,250 for single people. Then we urge a further exemption of $200 for dependent children.
There is one more tax to which I should like to refer, the tax on widows' incomes. Today under certain circumstances a widow who has brought up a family and who is maintaining a home is entitled to an exemption of only $750. She must maintain herself the same as a married person who has an exemption of $1,500. I submit to the minister that that exemption should be raised. At the age of 65 years the widow's exemption is by the Income Tax Act increased to $1,250, but we must remember that a widow who has brought up a family and who is maintaining a home may find her expenses just too heavy in the years before she reaches 65. I submit that the age limit should be reduced from 65 years to 50 years, so that the exemption would apply at the earlier age.
The Address-Mr. Timmins For the greater part of my time tonight I should like to speak on the subject of -the desperate need for housing in this country. In the face of increasing population-and there were over 83,000 new family formations in 1948-and in the face of increasing immigration-and there were over 125,000 new Canadians who came here last year-the Liberal government has assumed a negative and defeatist attitude to the production of housing in Canada. The records show that in 1946 only 65,000 houses were built. In 1947 the figures are 72,346 housing units, and in 1948 81,000 housing units. Of the number built last year only 26 per cent were rental units whereas rental accommodation is the type most in demand. As building costs go up, and the size of down payments increases, there are fewer and fewer people who can buy houses. Actually the builders who were building under the integrated housing plan have now run into certain difficulties.
The Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Winters) advised the house today of an amendment to the integrated housing plan, but I can tell him that, although his changes are laudatory, as a matter of fact they are not going to help the ordinary builder very much in building more houses in 1949. Some of the things that the minister has suggested, and which must have been given to him in good faith by his advisers, are rather difficult to accomplish in the housing business. I want to tell him that when he expects a builder part way through his job to present bills that have been paid and waivers of liens in respect of the job that is being performed he is asking for trouble. There is nothing more certain in the world than that he will run into trouble, if his department asks for that sort of thing. There are also new features of the National Housing Act which have caused trouble. I have seen clippings from the papers and I have had letters from builders who tell me that the National Housing Act is not working out to their satisfaction, and is not working out to the satisfaction of the general buying public. We are running into very serious difficulties in that regard at the very beginning of 1949.
We should remember that at least 90 per cent of the housing units which have been built in Canada in the last four years have been constructed by private builders. They have been constructed by private enterprise, and in spite of the building priority system because, and as a matter of fact, in most cases the builders get no priority at all for materials. They obtain materials wherever they can find them: The private builder has been carrying the load in spite of the government. It is my considered opinion that the problem of housing in Canada will only be solved

The Address-Mr. Timmins when the government gives private builders the materials to do the job, and gives them the green light to go ahead no matter what.
I should like to trace the attitude of the government on the question of housing as it has been indicated to the public since before the 1945 election. We can well remember those things that were said by cabinet ministers, and the promises that were made that, when the Liberal party was elected to power, houses would be turned out like tanks off a production line. They also said they had a housing program for Canada. The years have shown there is not any housing program for Canada. There has just been a series of expedients, of little things that are supposed to fit together, and they have not fitted together at all. There is no such thing as a housing plan for Canada even today.
Since 1945 we have heard the various utterances of the cabinet ministers and responsible parties. For a few minutes I am going to take the time to review them. The first was in July, 1947, and was a pronouncement of the then minister of reconstruction. He said: The government takes no responsibility for solving the entire housing problem for this country. It is perfectly ridiculous to suggest that it is a government responsibility. Every city has its own housing responsibility, as has every province. The government is responsible for the returned men, and its responsibility stops at that point.
I am going to suggest that the quotations I am about to give the house indicate that statement apparently still stands. "The government is responsible for the returned men, and its responsibility stops at that point."
In May of 1948 the then minister of reconstruction had this to say at page 3642 of Hansard:
Because of very high construction costs and because the building industry is now working at capacity, I do not think that the present is an opportune time to attempt the initial steps into the low-rental housing field. Certainly at this time I am not prepared to recommend capital subsidies or contributions to a rent reduction fund by the dominion.
To carry on a little further, the present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) became leader of his party, and very shortly afterwards he made a statement which has been quoted many times in the house, and which fits into the chronological order of the things I have to say. I will therefore read it. He said:
No government of which I am a part will ever pass legislation for subsidized housing.
He watered that down a short time afterwards, when he gave a press statement in which he said:
For the present the government will not consider subsidized housing for the low rental groups since it is convinced that no further money put into housing programs could build a single additional dwelling.

I wish to take issue violently with that statement because it shows a complete lack of knowledge of the subject. As a matter of fact, commencing in 1949 there are a good many factors which indicate that, given some leadership and direction, we could build a great many more houses in 1949 than were built in 1948. The first factor is that the lumber situation is a great deal easier. Throughout the country one can get lumber now, and it was hard to get last year. Then again labour is a good deal easier to secure. A year ago you could not get a labouring man on a building job. The boss had to do the labouring work himself. In addition to that, carpenters are now coming into the residential field. I know of one builder to whom three carpenters came in a period of two days within the last two months, and he took on two of them. The labour situation in residential building is getting better every day.
As to steel, from the information I receive, and the reports that come out from time to time, steel will be easier to obtain this year. By the third quarter of this year there will be a great deal of steel on the market. Steel goes into the manufacture of bathtubs, sinks, piping, hardware, and many other things that go to make up a house. In addition to all that, if we look at a little booklet, "Supply of Building Materials in Canada" which was sent to us by the Department of Trade and Commerce yesterday, we find at page 14 that they have this to say about building materials: Increased production of twenty-one of the thirty building materials covered here is anticipated in 1949.
I would say to the Prime Minister, if he were here, and I say to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply, who must now have these matters at his finger tips, that there is real hope for additional building in the year 1949. I have the temerity to say to him that if he wants any help from this side of the house and he thinks we can help him, and if he does not place too much weight upon what the Prime Minister tells him about the lack of building materials, or labour, or whatever it may be, we will give him the necessary advice, gratis.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to two paragraphs in the speech from the throne. The first is:
The provision of housing has received and continues to receive close attention. More new housing units were provided during the last calendar year than ever before.
That was in 1948, and we have no new thought for 1949 there.
Your approval will be sought for the establishment of a department of reconstruction and development

to continue the functions now vested in the Department of Reconstruction and Supply, including the ministerial responsibility for the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
The only new thought I can find in that paragraph is that this department now is going to be called the department of reconstruction and development. In other words, apparently the minister is going to be given some authority and some powers in respect of development. We on this side of the house admire the new minister very much and wish him good luck in the job he has undertaken, but I really feel he has just been handed a bag of tricks. I do not believe he has been given the authority he is entitled to. It seems to me, from the statement of the former minister of reconstruction, that this was not the time to start any new program, that this very direction or instruction has been handed on to the new minister, and he is stalled before he starts. He spoke in Toronto on January 24 of this year. Unfortunately I was not able to hear him, but I believe he made a very good speech. But in that speech he did not say anything new.
I was rather surprised, because those of us on this side expect to hear a lot of good things from him, a lot of new things. All he told the people was that about eighty thousand houses had been built last year and he hoped about one hundred thousand would be built in 1949. He also said that if we had one hundred thousand additional housing units available right now there would be occupants for every one of them. That is what we have been telling them on the other side, that we are one hundred thousand houses short.
Then the minister said something which some assistant must have put into his brief, I am sure. He said there was a sort of backlog of $100 million for public investment, which his department had to fall back on, some of which was going to be used in future for housing. Well, as a matter of fact we have all known about the public investment fund since 1944. I have seen letters saying to a certain industry, "We believe your project should fit into this public investment undertaking. When the proper time comes, if your project measures up we will see that you get some of this money". I know the minister is going to have some of that money to use for housing; but after all that is a hedge against bad times. I am sure none of those on the treasury benches and none of us on this side of the house are looking for those bad times to come, and we do not want to have to dig into this public investment fund for a long while, if ever. So there is nothing very much in the pronouncement of the minister that this fund is there, ready to fall back upon.
The Address-Mr. Timmins However, Mr. Speaker, I should like to get down to some other practical matters in respect of this housing situation, and to take you back to the city of Toronto for a few moments. In that city on or about May 1 or June 1 next there will be a bad time in housing by reason of the recent amendment to regulations under the wartime rental order. The report of the welfare commissioner is to the effect that more than 4,500 families will have been served with eviction notices, and that 1,000 families may soon require emergency accommodation which the city does not have. In my hand I have a picture of Little Norway, one of the places where many of these more or less displaced persons have been put, people who had to go into emergency housing. The only way you can get into this housing is through a foot of water. In this picture I see people paddling to their homes; I see children playing in the streets in rubber boots. Those are the conditions under which they are living.
The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) knows all about this. He was in Toronto two weeks ago and spoke at a civic dinner. He had been taken around to see these places, and in his speech he mentioned that it was unfortunate that these emergency shelter projects had to be carried on, but that they were only intended to be temporary and that something would have to be done about it. He made quite a good speech, to which I shall refer in a few minutes. As a matter of fact, the situation in Toronto can be duplicated all over the dominion. I am told that by June 1 perhaps 13,500 people in eastern Canada will have been served with these eviction notices, so it is easy to see where we are getting with respect to housing.
When the Prime Minister was in Toronto on February 19 he devoted every minute of his speech at the civic luncheon, about thirty-five minutes, to housing. So I do not need to tell the house that the right hon. gentleman is pretty well seized of this question. Last evening he also spoke on the national network, when again he had a good deal to say about housing. These are some of the things he said in Toronto, first with respect to housing for veterans:
Housing for veterans he admitted to be a national responsibility, but Mr. St. Laurent declared that "it is not a part of the present plans of the federal government to move from veterans' rental projects into rental housing for civilians."
As a matter of fact, if the government would only do something about veterans' houses, if they only had a plan about veterans' housing, if they would only start there and do something about it, then we could go on to the next paragraph. But they have no plan,

The Address-Mr. Timmins and there was nothing concrete in the speeches of the Prime Minister either last evening or in Toronto by way of a plan for veterans' housing. In the army we used to have a saying, "Let George do it." We have the same saying now in the party opposite. The fact of the matter is that in his speeches the Prime Minister really was saying, "Let George do it;" let the other fellow do it; let the municipality or the province do it. We will come to that in a moment, however. He also said:
"We feel that the proper policy for the federal government Is one which is limited to extending financial assistance to individuals and corporations, whether home owners or landlords."
Federal participation at present is limited to slum clearance grants and loans to limited dividend companies for low-rental housing, but the Prime Minister said that "it may be that experience will show that other forms of federal assistance will be desirable."
Well, Mr. Speaker, I point out that in what the Prime Minister has said, and in what the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Winters) has said either in or out of the house -and he has not really said very much about it in the house, though I presume he will do so later in this debate-there is nothing concrete by way of a plan for veterans, in the first place, and certainly there is nothing by way of a plan for any other citizens of our country. I quote further from his newspaper report:
The Prime Minister said his government is ready at any time to meet any provincial government In order to work out housing problems as between municipal, provincial and federal authorities.
In the house the other day the member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) asked the minister of reconstruction a question. He asked whether the government was willing to discuss long-range housing programs with any of the provincial representatives. The answer the minister gave, as reported in the press, is that he was not in favour of a dominion-provincial municipal conference on housing at this time. You see, Mr. Speaker, there is a certain amount of buck-passing taking place. The Prime Minister says the responsibility rests to some extent with the municipality. I am sure that each of the municipalities that have veterans who need houses would be willing to do its share. I am sure that every province in the country will be willing to do its share, too, but some leadership must be given. In so far as the veteran is concerned, the Prime Minister admits that the responsibility rests upon the federal government. Why can we not have a plan? Why can we not have a start? Why must we go around looking for someone to start the ball rolling?

I stand corrected if that was not the correct answer. Perhaps the minister would like to read it from Hansard now or when I have finished my speech.
A start must be made in all these things and I firmly believe that the start should be made in veterans' housing. I firmly believe that, if a start were made and we did have plans, the solution of the other problems connected with housing would follow right along. Something would then be done about emergency housing and, following that, would come the matter of slum clearance. In respect of all these matters, however, a start must be made.
The minister has also said, outside the house I believe, that he proposes to make a survey of housing in Canada so that he might know where to start. As a matter of fact, I presume every city and every town in Canada has a housing register. I believe such a survey could be made in a matter of two weeks. Certainly, it could be made by the end of this month. If housing is to be had in 1949, a start must be made almost right away. Following the survey I suggest that plans should be made immediately for the production of veterans' houses in every city and town in Canada where veterans' houses are needed. The Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has plans which have been going through its office for many years. This corporation has been dealing with the various expedients relating to housing such as land development, integrated housing plans, National Housing Act loans and all that sort of thing. I see no reason in the world why a plan for veterans' housing could not be produced within a matter of a few weeks after the survey is made.
Then, I think a conference of the mayors, provincial premiers or their deputies, along with the representatives of other municipal bodies should be called so that a start could be made, first of all, in respect of veterans' housing; secondly, for emergency housing; and thirdly, for slum clearance. I do think a start must be made now. Since we have a new minister and he has a new department with a new name, one word of which is "development"-which means dig, produce, erect, construct-all that is needed is more assistance from the treasury bench. The ability of the new minister should enable him to get that help. I do not often quote scripture here, but there is a verse in the

bible in which St. Paul is speaking to some of his followers in a distant city and he says:
Stand not upon the order of your going, but go at once.
I am saying to the minister that he should get started at once.

Mr. Speaker, the speech from the throne did not contain any legislation which might be termed controversial in nature. No doubt this is strategy on the part of the government since 1949 is likely to be an election year. The government candidates will find it sufficiently difficult to explain the policy of the government over the past three years without, at the same time, having to explain any controversial legislation which might have been disclosed in the speech from the throne.
It is unfortunate, however, that a side issue has been introduced into this debate, and that is dominion-provincial relations. I am not for one moment saying that dominion-provincial relations is not an important subject. It is. But I do insist there are before this government and before the country many other problems which should have precedence in this debate. One of those problems is the high cost of living in this country. I venture to say that the cost of living today is the main problem before the Canadian people. It is the main problem because it affects a larger number of people than any other problem in Canada. We have a housing problem and the possibility of an unemployment problem. We also have the problem of developing and finding markets for our agricultural products. At the moment, however, I insist that all those problems are subsidiary to the one problem of the high cost of living.
It is to be regretted that the government did not see fit to bring down legislation to deal with that all-important problem at this time. Reference has already been made in this debate to the high cost of living. As I say, it is unfortunate it did not receive more consideration. In previous sessions of this parliament, in 1946 and 1947, reference was also made to the high cost of living. Statements have been made by members in this house and by other people throughout the country that the reason for the high cost of living is the demands of labour for increased wages. I am not saying that when increases in wages are granted they will not increase the cost of living, but I do say that when people talk in that manner they should also give the other side of the picture. They should also deal with the extra profits obtained by large corporations which have also helped to raise the cost of living.
The Address-Mr. Moore
When these two subjects are considered side by side, I think it must be admitted that the increased profits of industry contributed a great deal more towards raising the cost of living than the increase in wages to the workingman. For a minute or two, I should like to develop that point. Unfortunately, I could not obtain figures dealing specifically with the Canadian situation. The figures I have, which deal with the situation in Canada, relate to one of our largest industries, namely, the iron and steel industry.
In the iron and steel industry, between 1945 and 1947, the workers received an increase in wages which amounted to nine per cent. During the same period of time the increase in the profits of the corporation amounted to sixty-six per cent. I submit that, when we are studying the reasons for the increase in the cost of living, we must give as much consideration to the increase in profits as to the increase in wages. I submit that up to the present time that has not been done. You can review the facts in connection with the pulp and paper industry, and a number of other industries in Canada, and you will find that the situation is similar to a greater or lesser degree; but the most important figures in connection with a study of this problem come from the United States. The Congress for Industrial Organization, one of the largest unions in the United States, has made a special study of this situation. They have carefully calculated how much a percentage increase in wages to the workers cost the plants which gave the increases. They have also calculated how much extra money the companies received by virtue of an increase in the price of the things which they had to sell. Here is the situation with respect to the United States, and I submit that I am being fair in presenting these figures for the United States, because the industrial picture of the United States is similar to the industrial picture in Canada. The standard of living in the two countries is somewhat similar, and generally speaking the economy of both countries is the same. Therefore, once again I submit that I am on solid ground when I say that the situation in the two countries can be considered on a par.
Take the iron and steel industry as an example. The iron and steel industry gave an increase in wages to their industrial workers, and at the same time an increase in the price of steel was given to the companies. The increase in wages cost the companies $170 million a year, but the increase in the price of steel netted the same companies $640 million a year extra.

The Address-Mr. Moore
Take the coal companies. They gave an increase in wages to their workers. That increase in wages cost these coal companies $150 million a year, but the increase in the price of coal netted the coal companies an additional $500 million a year.
Take the automobile manufacturers. Five of the largest corporations in the United States producing automobiles gave an increase in pay to their industrial workers. That increase in pay cost the companies $152 million a year; but, at the same time that the increase in pay was given, the price of automobiles was raised on the United States market, and that extra price netted the corporations an additional $540 million a year.
In calculating the increase in the cost of living in the United States you must take into consideration the fact that the owners of the industry get a much larger share of the excess prices than do the industrial workers, and that also explains the reason why we have a spiral in an inflationary period: A strike, an increase in wages, followed by another strike and an increase in wages.
I submit that the government have not dealt fairly with the people of this country because they have failed to deal with that situation. They have not dealt with the combines in this country. If all the legislation which is on the statute books of Canada to deal with the combines had been put into effect we should not have combines at this time. The first legislation enacted in Canada to deal with combines was enacted in 1889. Another act was put on the statute books in 1897. A combines investigation commission was set up in 1910. It was revised in 1919, and again revised in 1923. I believe a new act was brought into effect in 1935, amended in 1937 and again amended in 1945. After putting all that legislation on the statute books one would have thought that combines would not have got very far in Canada, but that is not so. The real problem before the people of Canada today is the control of these combines. I submit that both old parties have failed to bring about this control which would be in the interests of the average consumer in Canada.
I note one statement in the speech from the throne which said that there was a great danger in the world today from the spread of communism. Undoubtedly there is some truth in that statement; but I would have expected that the speech from the throne would contain another statement, namely, how they intended to deal with the situation in Canada. If they intended to deal with it, one of the first things that they would have said is, we are going to socialize or nationalize the large cartels and corporations which

are now in operation in Canada. If they had done that, they would have solved those problems which are the only ones that can lead to the development of communism in this country.
I am not a bit afraid of communism in this country. I am certain that it has not got a chance because the conditions which exist in Canada are entirely different from the conditions which existed in Russia at the time of the revolution, or the conditions which exist in China at the present time. A study of the economic factors in connection with these things will soon prove to anyone that communism cannot develop in a state as highly developed as Canada or the United States is today.
I now wish to deal for a moment with some of our other problems, some of the problems which I think should have been mentioned in the speech from the throne. It is often argued that the cost of living does not affect the farmer to the same extent that it affects the industrial worker. There may be some truth in that statement, but it must also be remembered that the cost of living has also increased for the farmer just as much as it has for the industrial worker, and more in some cases.
According to the bureau of statistics the average cost of living on farms today has increased by 38 per cent since 1945. But, in addition to that cost of living increase for the farmers, there is another increase, namely, an increase in the price of farm machinery and particularly an increase in the price of spare parts. It would naturally be argued that the farmer does not have to spend his money every year on renewing his machinery. That is quite true, but he must spend money every year to keep it up, and that involves the buying of spare parts. The costs of these spare parts at the present time are very high. I submit that the increased costs all the way down the line have taken from the people almost all that was gained during and after the war years in the increased level of operation of our national economy.
I am not going to review the history of the high cost of living; I am simply going to say that it is to be regretted the government saw fit to abandon price control at this time. The experiences of the government and the people of Canada were such as to prove that price control was the best possible method of maintaining the standard of living of the various groups throughout the country. You will remember, Mr. Speaker, when price control was lifted in 1947 on three hundred commodities in this country. These three hundred commodities were selected which did not figure too much in the actual cost of living. When the price ceilings were lifted the result

was a decided increase in the cost of living, sufficient to prove to this government and to anyone else that any abandonment of controls would lead to an unprecedented rise in the cost of living. But despite that information, which was available to everyone at the time, the government apparently yielded to the wishes of someone and gradually did away with price controls. In 1947 this was a pretty live issue. There was a possibility, when price controls were lifted, that great profits could be made from the sale of consumer goods. Naturally, some of our larger companies were extremely anxious that price control should be abandoned at the earliest possible moment. One of these gentlemen was the president of the Robert Simpson Company. This gentleman spoke to the shareholders of the company at a meeting in 1947. At that meeting he made this statement dealing with price control. I wish hon. members to listen to it, and decide who was more correct in judging the economic situation, the president of the Robert Simpson Company or the leaders of labour unions and leaders of farm organizations. Here is what the president had to say at that time:
An over-all and immediate lifting of ceilings would quickly react to the benefit of all consumers. The considerations which the government took into account as necessary in applying the over-all price ceiling in 1941, are now working to the disadvantage of consumers. In spite of subsidies, in some cases running into hundreds of thousands a year, standard lines at popular prices, many of them household and personal essentials, have not been produced except in token quantities, simply because a producer could keep workers employed making substitute articles which could be made at a profit in spite of the price ceiling.
And it goes on:
Even if these standard popular priced lines were produced to sell at a price somewhat higher than the ceiling the real cost of living would be less in total than at present. There has been such continuous propaganda on one side of this question that it is difficult for many to believe the truth of this "price" situation.
In view of what has happened since that speech was made, I leave it to any hon. member to decide who was the more correct, the president of that company or the leaders of the unions and farm organizations throughout Canada. With the cost of living where it is today, our decision can go only in one direction-against the company.
I should like now to say a few words in connection with agricultural marketing. Despite the expansion of our industrial production in Canada, agriculture remains our basic and our chief industry. It is also true, however, that agriculture depends to a very large degree upon a foreign market to maintain the standard of living of our agricultural producers and workers. At the present time almost 50 per cent of our agricultural pro-
The Address-Mr. Moore duction must go abroad. That means we must have a foreign market to take delivery of those goods.
At the present time, I believe, the British foreign market is the best possible market we can develop for our agricultural products. I believe that, not because I am of British parentage, but because Britain is the largest single market anywhere in the world for the delivery of agricultural products. I think all possible steps should now be taken to develop that market to the utmost for our agricultural industry.
At the present time there are great trading difficulties between this country and Great Britain, something which has been termed a dollar shortage. Britain's purchases from Canada are limited to the availability of United States dollars. At the present time it would appear that Great Britain may even have to cut down on her imports from this country.
A few days ago I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) if the government thought there was any possibility of Britain's adopting an austerity program toward this country because of her unfavourable balance of trade. He replied that he did not think there was that possibility. However, in view of the fact that, when we had an unfavourable balance of trade with the United States, we adopted an austerity program toward that country, I do feel the government here should immediately take steps to deal with the trading situation which exists between this country and Great Britain and do everything possible to retain the British market for the sale of agricultural products.
I should like to take a few minutes to express again a view which has been expressed by other hon. members. I do so because I think it is of extreme importance to the agricultural industry in western Canada. A few days ago the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) and the member for Skeena spoke about the necessity for developing barter trade between this country and Great Britain. I want fully to support what the hon. members said in that connection. I feel quite firmly that this government should take all possible steps toward developing a long-term agreement with Great Britain on a barter basis. I am not going to say for what period of time the trade contract should be made; but if the British government feel they would "like a ten-year contract, I would say we should go ahead and arrange a contract on the basis best suited to them. Once again we must remember that the British market is the largest single market in the world, and the easiest

The Address-Mr. Moore one to develop so far as Canadian agricultural products are concerned.
Then, in connection with foreign trade,
I should like to advance another argument. I am sure hon. members on all sides of the house are aware of the great development now taking place in India. Since the end of the war India has become a self-governing dominion. It is true that part of the country has divided itself from the other, and set up a separate government in Pakistan. Nevertheless great developments are taking place in that country. Iron and steel mills are being built. Textile plants are being built. A pulp and paper industry is being developed.
I am told that just recently the government of Pakistan has undertaken to institute a housing program, if you please; and that within eight years they hope to build approximately a million homes in that country. If this development takes place it will raise considerably the standard of living of the people in that country, with the result that there will be available a very sizeable market for the export of goods from this country; and I urge the government to bend every effort toward developing trade with India. If their standard of living is increased, the huge population of that country would provide a great market not only for Canada but for other countries as well.
I should like now to say a few words concerning the importance of the housing problem in this country. A number of speakers in the debate have already dealt with that subject; and at the risk of repeating what has been said already I shall deal with it for a few moments. It is important to remember that housing is not a problem of recent years in Canada. If anyone is interested, he or she may go down to the parliamentary library and look at newspapers as far back as 1911 which reveal that a housing problem has existed in Canada since that time.
There are editorials in the Montreal papers of 1911 which deplore the fact that in that year slums were developing in the principal cities of Canada-Montreal, Vancouver and Toronto. The problem was not solved during the first world war, and was not solved in the years between the two wars. In 1938 we were still short by some 400,000 of the number of housing units required in Canada. In addition to that, according to the Curtis report there were another 175,000 homes which could be described as slums and which ought to have been destroyed and rebuilt.
Why is it that ever since 1911 we have not had sufficient homes adequately to house our people? I believe the reason is that there was not a large enough percentage of the working people of Canada with sufficient


means to build homes. According to the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, the average income of 45 per cent of our population does not come within any taxation bracket. Those are the people in Canada who are not in possession of homes. According to the same authorities, less than one-third of the people in Canada receive incomes greater than $2,100 per year. So the construction of homes in this country is limited to that small group of people whose incomes are above $2,100 per year. From 20 to 25 per cent of the working people in Canada have to provide homes sufficient for the whole of the country. Our experience in the past has proved that it cannot be done.
If we are to have sufficient homes in this country they can be provided only by the institution of a national housing program. That program will have to be put into effect by co-operation between the federal government, the various provincial governments and the local municipal authorities. Until that is done our housing problem will still be with us.
There is another point I should like to consider in connection with this housing program. The argument is often advanced that it will cost a great deal of money to carry forward this program. That is true, but at the present time the federal government is spending a great deal of money on a national health program-I want to hasten to say that I am thoroughly in agreement with it-but if nothing is done about our serious housing problem we will soon approach the time when the lack of housing will jeopardize the success of the national health program.
If this problem is to be solved, I urge that action be taken along the lines of the recommendations of the Canadian welfare council. I am going to quote the recommendations of that council because they have made a thorough study of Canada's housing problem and I think the recommendations will be of some concern and of much interest to hon. members in this house. They are as follows:
(1)	The objective of national housing policy should be a supply of housing sufficient to provide a decent home in a healthy environment for every Canadian family. The responsibility of the national government does not cease until this objective has been gained.
(2)	In order to overcome the high costs of residential building the federal government should:
(a)	Intensify its research activities for the development of more economical and efficient fabrication techniques.
(b)	Finance the establishment of industries for producing and assembling houses.
(3)	In order to overcome the lack of decent housing available to low income families and their incapacity to pay for new housing, the federal government should inaugurate a long-term program of public housing with the co-operation of the pro-

vincial and municipal authorities. This program should be started immediately in order that the whole administrative organization may be put into action in readiness for further expansion when required. For this purpose:
(a)	A national rent reduction fund should be established.
(b)	The loan facilities of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation should be made available to local public housing authorities to be established by the municipalities.
(4)	The provincial government should provide enabling legislation for the establishment of local public housing authorities and define their areas of operation so as to encourage the greatest possible collaboration with local planning boards. Provincial governments should also be prepared to operate housing projects in rural areas and wherever local governments are inadequately equipped to assume such responsibilities.
(5)	The local housing authorities so established should assume responsibility for the development, ownership and management of public housing estates and should assume control of the wartime housing projects and other publicly owned housing within their communities.
(6)	The public housing program should be expanded and developed in such a manner and at such times that the nation's supply of new housing may be maintained at the required volume and so that the plant and personnel of the residential building industry may be kept in continuous operation.
I should like to say one word in connection with this proposed national housing program. If such a program is set up its purpose should be, first, to take care of the serious backlog of housing needs that exists in Canada at the present time. When that problem has been coped with, then arrangements should be made to meet the annual requirements of the nation out of new production. If that were done I believe it would contribute a great deal to the success of the national health program.
I want to say a word about a problem which exists in my constituency. I took this matter up last year with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) and also with the provincial department of education of Manitoba, but I regret to say that as far as I know no action has been taken up to the present time.

I rise at this time to deal chiefly with the shelf of public projects in the Department of Reconstruction and Supply. I do so because of the fact that I recently tabled some information in the house and several members have commented that the government has, to quote one of them, "a meagre, puny and inadequate plan to deal with the potential unemployment in this country". If this shelf of public projects were the government's overall plan for dealing with potential unemployment in this country, I would heartily concur in the sentiment expressed. That, however, is not the case. The building up of a reserve shelf of public projects is only a part of the government's policy for maintaining high levels of employment and income. Another aspect of that policy, and closely related to public investment, is the encouraging of private investors, by tax concessions and credit provision, to take advantage of the tremendous field of industrial expansion that is still ahead of us, and to improve the

The Address-Mr. Winters amenities of life by better housing, well planned communities, and the enlargement and improvement of facilities for social and cultural development. To help maintain high levels of employment and income, the government is also helping substantially to increase the economic stability of the internal economy by such means as floor prices on farm and fish products, and special assistance to industries that are encountering difficulties. Recent examples of this are assistance to gold producers, the establishment of the maritime commission and the coal board, and the government's proposal to assist the production of steel. In that connection I refer to the speech from the throne, and I read:
You will be asked to make legislative provision for governmental assistance by loan to the producers of basic steel for the purpose of increasing production.
The government is also seeking to assure favourable and expanding markets abroad for our surplus production by supporting international efforts to unfetter world trade, and much has already been done directly by export credits and export credit insurance. Finally, the social security measures of the present government, unemployment insurance, family allowances and pensions for the aged and the blind, by increasing the stability of personal income, would help maintain consumer spending if we should run into a period of recession. This many-sided approach to the problems of employment and unemployment was the basic program laid down in the white paper of 1945.
The hon. member for Saskatoon City (Mr. Knight), who expressed the opinion that the shelf of public projects was meagre and puny, also stated that "the famous white paper on reconstruction held out hope for a tremendous program of public works for any possible period of unemployment". I find nowhere in the white paper where the hope is held out of "a tremendous program of public works". On the contrary, what I do find is the statement that "the post-war employment problem is not to be solved by huge expenditures on 'public works'. Efforts to increase and stabilize employment and income must pervade all economic policies".
